title: Iliad
creator: Homer
location: Oral composition in Ionia; fixed in writing perhaps 7th–6th century BC
description: The Iliad is an epic of about 15,700 lines of dactylic hexameter, set during a few weeks in the tenth year of the Greek siege of Troy. It opens with a quarrel between Agamemnon, leader of the Greeks, and their greatest warrior, Achilles, who withdraws from the fighting in anger. Without him the Greeks are driven back to their ships, until the death of his beloved companion Patroclus at the hands of the Trojan prince Hector brings Achilles back in murderous grief. He kills Hector and abuses his corpse, but the poem ends with a scene of reconciliation when the aged king Priam comes to ransom his son's body. Built from formulaic phrases and type scenes inherited from oral tradition, the poem combines brutal battlefield detail with long similes drawn from peaceful life and an extraordinary sympathy for both sides. It was the foundation of Greek education, a model for Virgil and Milton, and is still read in new translations as a profound meditation on war, honour and mortality.

title: Odyssey
creator: Homer
location: Oral composition in Ionia; fixed in writing perhaps 7th–6th century BC
description: The Odyssey, in twenty-four books of hexameter verse, tells of the homecoming of Odysseus, king of Ithaca, after the fall of Troy. It begins with his son Telemachus searching for news of him while suitors devour the household and press his mother Penelope to remarry. Odysseus, held for years by the nymph Calypso, reaches the court of the Phaeacians and there recounts his wanderings: the Cyclops Polyphemus, the witch Circe, the descent to the underworld, the Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis. Returning disguised as a beggar, he tests his household and, with Telemachus, kills the suitors before being reunited with Penelope. The poem's complex structure, with its flashbacks and stories within stories, and its hero who survives by cunning rather than strength made it the model for countless later narratives. Its episodes have become part of common language, and its influence runs from Virgil and Dante to Joyce's Ulysses and modern novels and films.

title: Ode to Aphrodite (Fragment 1)
creator: Sappho
location: Lesbos; preserved in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, 1st century BC
description: The Ode to Aphrodite is the only one of Sappho's poems known to survive complete, preserved because the critic Dionysius of Halicarnassus quoted it in full in the first century BC as an example of polished style. Written in seven Sapphic stanzas, it takes the form of a hymn: the poet calls on Aphrodite to come to her, as she has before, and recalls a previous visit when the goddess descended in a chariot drawn by sparrows, smiled and asked whom she should persuade to love Sappho this time. The goddess promises that the one who flees will soon pursue. The poem blends ritual prayer with personal desire and gentle self-mockery, and is notable for naming the speaker as Sappho. Together with the fragment known as Sappho 31, which describes the physical symptoms of desire, it has been among the most imitated and translated lyric poems in Western literature.

title: Oresteia
creator: Aeschylus
location: First performed at the Great Dionysia, Athens, where it won first prize
description: The Oresteia consists of three tragedies first staged together in Athens in 458 BC, two years before Aeschylus's death. In Agamemnon, the king returns victorious from Troy and is murdered in his bath by his wife Clytemnestra, in revenge for his sacrifice of their daughter Iphigenia. In The Libation Bearers, their son Orestes returns from exile and, commanded by Apollo, kills his mother and her lover Aegisthus. In The Eumenides, Orestes is pursued by the Furies, spirits of vengeance, to Athens, where the goddess Athena sets up a court, the Areopagus, to try him. The jury is evenly divided and Athena's vote acquits him; the Furies are persuaded to become benevolent guardians of the city. The trilogy has been read as a drama of the movement from private vendetta to public justice, and it raises questions about gender and authority that still provoke debate. Its massive choral odes and imagery of nets, blood and light are among the summits of Greek poetry.

title: Prometheus Bound
creator: Aeschylus
location: Athens (date and circumstances of first performance unknown)
description: Prometheus Bound shows the Titan Prometheus being nailed to a crag in the Caucasus by Might, Violence and the reluctant smith-god Hephaestus, as punishment for stealing fire from the gods and giving it to humanity, along with all the arts of civilisation. Chained in place, he receives a series of visitors, among them the chorus of the daughters of Oceanus and the wandering Io, also a victim of Zeus, and reveals that he knows a secret that could overthrow the new ruler of the gods. Refusing to disclose it to Hermes, he is plunged into the abyss amid thunder and earthquake as the play ends. It was traditionally the first part of a trilogy by Aeschylus, but many scholars now doubt his authorship on grounds of style and metre. Whoever wrote it, the image of Prometheus as defiant benefactor of mankind inspired Goethe, Byron, Percy Shelley's Prometheus Unbound and Mary Shelley's Frankenstein, subtitled The Modern Prometheus.

title: Antigone
creator: Sophocles
location: First performed in Athens
description: Antigone is set in Thebes after a civil war in which Oedipus's sons Eteocles and Polynices have killed each other. Their uncle Creon, now king, decrees that Polynices, who attacked the city, must lie unburied. Their sister Antigone defies him, sprinkling earth on the body in obedience to the gods' unwritten laws, and when caught refuses to repent. Creon condemns her to be walled up alive in a cave, ignoring the pleas of his son Haemon, her betrothed, and the warnings of the prophet Tiresias. When he finally relents, it is too late: Antigone has hanged herself, Haemon kills himself over her body, and Creon's wife Eurydice takes her own life. The play's clash between individual conscience and state authority, and between two people each partly in the right, as Hegel argued, has made it one of the most discussed works of drama. It has been rewritten in new political contexts by Anouilh, Brecht and many others.

title: Medea
creator: Euripides
location: First performed at the Great Dionysia, Athens, where it placed third
description: Medea is set in Corinth, where Jason, leader of the Argonauts, has brought Medea, the princess from Colchis who helped him win the Golden Fleece and betrayed her own family for him. Now he has abandoned her to marry the daughter of King Creon, and Creon orders her into exile. Medea, a foreigner and a woman with no rights, pretends to accept her fate, sends the bride a poisoned robe and crown that kill her and her father, and then, after a famous monologue in which she struggles with herself, murders her two sons to destroy Jason completely. She escapes in a chariot of the sun god. The play shocked and puzzled its first audience but has become one of the most performed Greek tragedies. Its speeches on the position of women, foreignness and betrayal, and its terrifying, sympathetic heroine, have inspired versions by Seneca, Corneille, Cherubini and countless modern writers.

title: Oedipus the King (Oedipus Rex)
creator: Sophocles
location: First performed at the Great Dionysia, Athens
description: Oedipus the King opens with Thebes stricken by plague. The oracle at Delphi declares that the city must expel the murderer of the former king Laius, and Oedipus, the clever outsider who saved Thebes by solving the riddle of the Sphinx, vows to find him. Step by step, through the blind prophet Tiresias, his wife Jocasta, a messenger from Corinth and an old shepherd, he uncovers the truth: he is Laius's son, abandoned at birth, who unknowingly killed his father on the road and married his mother. Jocasta hangs herself and Oedipus blinds himself with her brooches. The play is a masterpiece of construction, in which every step towards knowledge brings disaster nearer, and its dramatic irony is relentless. Aristotle treated it as the ideal tragedy, with reversal and recognition coinciding. Freud took from it the name of the Oedipus complex, and it has been endlessly translated, staged and adapted.

title: Lysistrata
creator: Aristophanes
location: First performed in Athens, probably at the Lenaia festival
description: Lysistrata was staged in 411 BC, during the long war between Athens and Sparta and shortly after Athens's disastrous expedition to Sicily. The Athenian woman Lysistrata persuades the women of the warring Greek cities to refuse sex to their husbands until they make peace, while the older women seize the Acropolis and its treasury. A chorus of old men tries to smoke them out and is drenched with water by a chorus of old women. The strike is hard on both sides, with much bawdy comedy as wives slip away and husbands suffer, but in the end the desperate Athenian and Spartan envoys agree to peace, and the play ends in celebration. Behind the obscene farce lies a serious plea for reconciliation. Lysistrata has been one of the most frequently revived Greek comedies in modern times, often staged as an anti-war play.

title: The Bacchae
creator: Euripides
location: First performed posthumously at the Great Dionysia, Athens, where it won first prize
description: The Bacchae was written in Macedonia in the last years of Euripides's life and staged after his death. Dionysus, god of wine, ecstasy and theatre, arrives at Thebes disguised as a mortal stranger to establish his rites in the city of his mother Semele, whose sisters denied his divinity. He has driven the women of Thebes into a frenzy on Mount Cithaeron. The young king Pentheus tries to suppress the cult and imprisons the stranger, but the god escapes, breaks Pentheus's will and leads him, dressed as a woman, to spy on the women. There they tear him apart, led by his own mother Agave, who returns carrying his head in triumph before she comes to her senses. The play, with its magnificent choral odes, is a disturbing study of religious ecstasy, repression and the irrational. It was a central text for Nietzsche's ideas about the Dionysian and is among the most frequently staged Greek tragedies today.

title: The Frogs
creator: Aristophanes
location: First performed at the Lenaia festival, Athens, where it won first prize
description: The Frogs was staged in 405 BC, shortly after the deaths of Euripides and Sophocles and in the last desperate year of Athens's war with Sparta. Dionysus, patron of the theatre, laments that there are no good poets left and sets off to the underworld, disguised as Heracles and accompanied by his slave Xanthias, to bring Euripides back. Crossing the lake of the dead, he is mocked by a chorus of croaking frogs. In Hades he finds a contest under way between Aeschylus and Euripides for the throne of tragedy, and he presides over a hilarious debate in which they parody each other's verses and weigh them on a scale. In the end Dionysus chooses Aeschylus as the poet who can save the city. The play is one of the earliest works of literary criticism, a precious source for how Athenians thought about tragedy, and it was so admired that it was given a second performance.

title: Georgics
creator: Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro)
location: Rome
description: The Georgics is a poem of about 2,200 hexameter lines in four books, written in the years after the civil wars, when Italy's countryside lay ravaged and Octavian was establishing his rule. Nominally a farming manual in the tradition of Hesiod, it covers crops and weather, the cultivation of vines and olives, cattle and horses, and beekeeping. It is also a meditation on labour, on Italy, on the relation between humans and nature and on the violence of history; the first book ends with a vision of the omens that followed Caesar's assassination. The fourth book closes with the story of Aristaeus and the myth of Orpheus and Eurydice, one of the most celebrated passages in Latin poetry. Dryden called it the best poem of the best poet, and it has shaped writing about the countryside from Renaissance poets to Wordsworth and modern nature writing.

title: Odes (Carmina)
creator: Horace (Quintus Horatius Flaccus)
location: Rome
description: Horace published three books of Odes in 23 BC and added a fourth around 13 BC. In them he set out to do in Latin what Sappho, Alcaeus and Pindar had done in Greek, adapting their complex metres with unmatched skill. The poems are addressed to friends, lovers, patrons, gods and the emperor, and range from light invitations to drinking parties and love affairs to grand public odes on Rome's moral renewal under Augustus. Their recurrent theme is the brevity of life and the wisdom of enjoying the present moderately, crystallised in the phrase carpe diem, seize the day, from Ode 1.11. Horace ends Book 3 with the boast that he has built a monument more lasting than bronze. The Odes were imitated by Petrarch, Ronsard, Ben Jonson, Marvell and Pope and translated countless times, and they became the model for the classical ode in European poetry.

title: Aeneid
creator: Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro)
location: Rome; published posthumously by order of Augustus
description: The Aeneid is an epic of twelve books in Latin hexameter, left unfinished at Virgil's death and published on the orders of the emperor Augustus. Its first half recalls the Odyssey: Aeneas, escaping the fall of Troy with his father and son, wanders the Mediterranean, is shipwrecked at Carthage, tells Queen Dido the story of Troy's destruction and becomes her lover, until the gods order him to leave and Dido kills herself. After visiting the underworld, where his father shows him the future heroes of Rome, he reaches Italy, and the second half, like the Iliad, narrates his war against the Latin hero Turnus, ending abruptly when Aeneas kills him in anger. The poem celebrates Rome's destiny and Augustus's peace, yet it is shadowed throughout by loss, the cost of empire and the suffering of the defeated. It was Europe's central school text for nearly two thousand years and shaped the epic tradition of Dante, Tasso and Milton.

title: Metamorphoses
creator: Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso)
location: Rome (completed as Ovid went into exile)
description: The Metamorphoses is a poem of fifteen books in hexameter, which Ovid completed around AD 8, just as Augustus banished him to the Black Sea. It strings together roughly 250 myths linked by the theme of change of shape, in a continuous story running from the creation of the cosmos out of chaos through the age of gods and heroes and the Trojan War to the founding of Rome and the transformation of Julius Caesar into a star. Among its stories are Apollo and Daphne, Narcissus and Echo, Pyramus and Thisbe, Phaethon, Arachne, Daedalus and Icarus, Orpheus and Eurydice, and Pygmalion. Ovid moves from one tale to the next with brilliant transitions and tells them with wit, irony, eroticism and psychological insight. For medieval and Renaissance readers it was the main handbook of classical mythology, and its influence on Chaucer, Shakespeare, Titian, Bernini and countless later artists is incalculable.

title: Beowulf
creator: The Beowulf poet
location: Surviving manuscript: Nowell Codex, c. 1000, British Library, London
description: Beowulf is an Old English poem of 3,182 alliterative lines, surviving in a single manuscript copied around the year 1000 and badly damaged in the Cotton Library fire of 1731. It is set in sixth-century Scandinavia. The young Geatish warrior Beowulf sails to Denmark to help King Hrothgar, whose hall Heorot is attacked nightly by the monster Grendel. Beowulf tears off Grendel's arm, then follows Grendel's vengeful mother to her lair beneath a lake and kills her. Fifty years later, as king of the Geats, he fights a dragon that is ravaging his land, killing it with the help of the young Wiglaf but dying of his wounds; the poem ends with his funeral pyre and the lament of his people. Rich in digressions on feuds and old kings, kennings and elegiac reflection, it shows a Christian poet looking back on a pagan heroic world. It was little studied until the nineteenth century and is now the foundational work of English literature, translated by poets including Seamus Heaney.

title: The Song of Roland
creator: Turold
location: Oldest manuscript: Bodleian Library, Oxford (Digby 23), 12th century
description: The Song of Roland is the oldest major work of French literature, a poem of about 4,000 ten-syllable lines in stanzas linked by assonance. It transforms a minor historical event, the ambush of Charlemagne's rearguard by Basques in the Pyrenees in 778, into a crusading epic of Christians against Saracens. The traitor Ganelon, out of hatred for his stepson Roland, arranges for the rearguard to be attacked at the pass of Roncevaux by an immense Muslim army. Roland, proud and brave, refuses his friend Oliver's pleas to blow his horn, the oliphant, to recall the emperor, and when he finally does, it is too late; he dies facing Spain, offering his glove to God. Charlemagne returns to avenge him, defeats the Saracens and has Ganelon executed. The poem is written in a stark, formal style with repeated scenes and phrases. It shaped ideals of chivalry and became the basis of Italian romance epics by Boiardo and Ariosto.

title: Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart
creator: Chrétien de Troyes
location: Court of Marie de Champagne, Troyes
description: Lancelot, or the Knight of the Cart was written by Chrétien de Troyes, by his own account on a subject and treatment supplied by his patron Marie de Champagne. When Queen Guinevere is abducted by Meleagant to the land of Gorre, from which no one returns, an unnamed knight sets out to rescue her. Having lost his horse, he hesitates for two steps before climbing into a cart used to carry criminals, a public disgrace; he is later revealed as Lancelot. He crosses a bridge made of a sword blade, frees the queen and spends a night with her, but she rebukes him for his moment of hesitation. The poem is the earliest surviving story of the love of Lancelot and Guinevere, and its picture of a knight utterly obedient to his lady became a central text of courtly love. Chrétien left it to another poet, Godefroi de Leigny, to finish. Its themes entered the great prose Lancelot cycle and, through Malory, the English Arthurian tradition.

title: Perceval, the Story of the Grail
creator: Chrétien de Troyes
location: Written for Philip, count of Flanders
description: Perceval, or the Story of the Grail was Chrétien's last romance, dedicated to Philip of Flanders and left unfinished at about 9,000 lines, perhaps because of the poet's death. Perceval, raised by his widowed mother in the forest, ignorant of chivalry, sets out for King Arthur's court and becomes a knight. At the castle of the wounded Fisher King he witnesses a strange procession, including a bleeding lance and a richly decorated grail, a serving dish, but out of misplaced politeness fails to ask whom the grail serves. He later learns that his silence has prevented the king's healing. The romance then follows Arthur's nephew Gawain's adventures before breaking off. Chrétien's grail was not yet the cup of the Last Supper, an idea added by Robert de Boron and others. Four verse continuations tried to finish the story, and it inspired Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival, the Holy Grail legend and, much later, Wagner's Parsifal.

title: La Vita Nuova
creator: Dante Alighieri
location: Florence
description: La Vita Nuova, The New Life, is Dante's first book, assembled in Florence a few years after the death of Beatrice Portinari in 1290. It combines thirty-one poems, sonnets, canzoni and a ballata, with a prose narrative and commentary explaining the circumstances of each poem and analysing its structure. Dante tells how he first saw Beatrice when they were both nine, how she greeted him nine years later, how he hid his love behind screen ladies, and how her death plunged him into grief and then led him towards a spiritual understanding of love. The book ends with a vision and his resolve to write of her what had never been said of any woman, a promise fulfilled in the Divine Comedy. It is the finest work of the dolce stil novo, the sweet new style of Tuscan love poetry, and an early example of autobiographical fiction. The Pre-Raphaelite Dante Gabriel Rossetti translated it into English.

title: Divine Comedy
creator: Dante Alighieri
location: Written in exile in Verona and Ravenna; first printed in Foligno, 1472
description: Dante called his poem simply the Commedia, because it begins in misery and ends in joy; the epithet divine was added by Boccaccio and appeared on a Venetian edition of 1555. Written in exile over more than a decade, it consists of a hundred cantos in terza rima, a rhyme scheme Dante invented, divided into Inferno, Purgatorio and Paradiso. Lost in a dark wood in the Easter week of 1300, Dante is rescued by the poet Virgil, who leads him down through the nine circles of Hell, where sinners suffer punishments that mirror their sins, and up the mountain of Purgatory, where souls are purified. At its summit Beatrice, the woman he loved, takes over and guides him through the heavenly spheres to a vision of God. The poem is a vast synthesis of medieval theology, philosophy, astronomy and politics, populated with historical and contemporary figures, from Francesca da Rimini and Ulysses to popes and Florentine enemies. Written in Tuscan, it helped create the Italian language, and its images of the afterlife have shaped Western imagination ever since.

title: The Decameron
creator: Giovanni Boccaccio
location: Florence; earliest autograph manuscript in the Staatsbibliothek, Berlin
description: The Decameron, whose Greek-derived title means ten days, opens with a harrowing description of the plague that struck Florence in 1348. Seven young women and three young men meet in the church of Santa Maria Novella and decide to retreat to the countryside, where they pass the time with music, dancing and storytelling. Each day one of them is chosen as king or queen and sets a theme, and each tells one tale, so that a hundred stories are told in all. They range from bawdy tricks played on husbands and corrupt clergy to tales of wit, generosity, love and tragedy, such as the story of the patient Griselda, which ends the collection. Boccaccio's clear, flexible prose established Italian as a literary language for prose as Dante had for verse. The book was often censored, but it became one of the most influential works of European literature, mined by Chaucer, Shakespeare, Lope de Vega, Molière and Keats, and filmed by Pasolini.

title: Il Canzoniere (Rerum vulgarium fragmenta)
creator: Petrarch (Francesco Petrarca)
location: Final autograph manuscript: Vatican Library (Vat. lat. 3195)
description: Petrarch called his collection of Italian poems Rerum vulgarium fragmenta, fragments in the vernacular, and worked on its selection and order for decades until his death; the final arrangement survives partly in his own hand. It contains 366 poems, 317 of them sonnets, together with canzoni, sestinas, ballate and madrigals. They trace his love for Laura, first seen in Avignon in 1327, through the years of her life and, after her death in the plague of 1348, through mourning, memory and a final turn to the Virgin Mary. Petrarch explores the contradictions of love, burning and freezing, hope and despair, in polished language rich in paradox, puns on Laura's name and images of the laurel. The collection perfected the Italian sonnet and created the conventions of Petrarchism, which spread across Europe in the sixteenth century through Bembo, Ronsard, Garcilaso, Wyatt and Sidney and shaped Shakespeare's sonnets.

title: Troilus and Criseyde
creator: Geoffrey Chaucer
location: London
description: Troilus and Criseyde is a poem of more than eight thousand lines in rhyme royal stanzas, adapted from Boccaccio's Il Filostrato and often considered Chaucer's finest completed work. During the siege of Troy, the young prince Troilus mocks lovers until he falls helplessly in love with the widow Criseyde. Her uncle Pandarus brings them together, and in the central books their love is consummated in a scene of great tenderness. When Criseyde is exchanged for a Trojan prisoner and sent to her father in the Greek camp, she promises to return within ten days, but alone and afraid she accepts the Greek warrior Diomede. Troilus is killed in battle and from the eighth sphere laughs at the vanity of earthly love. Chaucer's sympathetic, ambiguous portrayal of Criseyde and his narrator's anxious commentary give the poem a psychological depth that has led some critics to call it the first English novel. Shakespeare used the story for his Troilus and Cressida.

title: The Canterbury Tales
creator: Geoffrey Chaucer
type: Collection of verse and prose tales
location: Earliest manuscripts: Hengwrt (National Library of Wales) and Ellesmere (Huntington Library), c. 1400–1410
description: The Canterbury Tales is Chaucer's unfinished masterpiece, written in Middle English in the last fifteen years of his life. In the General Prologue, some thirty pilgrims gather at the Tabard Inn in Southwark before setting off for the shrine of Thomas Becket at Canterbury, and the innkeeper proposes that each should tell stories on the way, with a free supper for the best. Chaucer sketches them with sharp, humorous detail: the Knight, the Prioress, the Miller, the Wife of Bath, the Pardoner and others from nearly every rank of society. Only twenty-four tales were completed, and they range across every medieval genre, from chivalric romance and saints' lives to bawdy fabliaux, beast fable and sermon, each suited to its teller, with lively quarrels between them. Most are in iambic pentameter couplets, a form Chaucer pioneered in English. Printed by William Caxton around 1476, the Tales became the foundation of English poetry and remain the most widely read work of medieval English literature.

title: Gargantua and Pantagruel
creator: François Rabelais
location: Lyon (first two books) and Paris
description: Gargantua and Pantagruel is a sequence of five books published from 1532, beginning with Pantagruel and followed by Gargantua (1534), which tells the story of Pantagruel's father, then the Third Book (1546), the Fourth Book (1552) and a posthumous Fifth Book of uncertain authenticity. Loosely based on a popular chapbook about giants, it follows the birth, monstrous appetites and education of Gargantua and his son Pantagruel, Gargantua's war against the ridiculous king Picrochole, the founding of the anti-monastery of Thélème, and the voyages of Pantagruel and his rascally companion Panurge in search of an answer to whether Panurge should marry. Rabelais filled the books with obscene humour, lists, invented words, parodies of legal and theological jargon and serious humanist ideas about education and peace. They were condemned by the Sorbonne but read across Europe, and they added the adjective Rabelaisian to many languages.

title: Essays
creator: Michel de Montaigne
location: Bordeaux (first edition, two books, 1580); Paris (1588; posthumous edition 1595)
description: Montaigne published the first two books of his Essais in Bordeaux in 1580, and an enlarged edition with a third book in Paris in 1588; he continued to annotate his own copy until his death, and the posthumous edition of 1595 incorporated many additions. The 107 chapters vary from a page to a hundred pages and range over subjects such as friendship, education, cannibals, cruelty, the power of the imagination, experience and death. Montaigne writes in a candid, conversational and digressive style, constantly quoting ancient authors and testing their ideas against his own experience, habits and contradictions, because, as he says in his preface, he himself is the matter of his book. His scepticism and tolerance, at the height of the French Wars of Religion, were radical. The Essays invented a literary form and profoundly influenced Shakespeare, Bacon, Pascal, Rousseau, Emerson and Nietzsche, and they remain a model for personal writing.

title: Doctor Faustus
creator: Christopher Marlowe
location: First performed in London (1594 is the first recorded performance); printed 1604
description: The Tragical History of the Life and Death of Doctor Faustus is based on a German chapbook about the legendary magician Johann Faust, translated into English around 1592. Faustus, a brilliant scholar at Wittenberg dissatisfied with philosophy, medicine, law and theology, turns to magic and signs a contract in his own blood with Lucifer, through the devil Mephistopheles, in exchange for twenty-four years of service. He uses his powers for tricks at the papal court and before the emperor and summons Helen of Troy, but he wavers between repentance and despair, and in the great final soliloquy waits in terror for the clock to strike midnight before the devils carry him off. The play survives in two different early texts, of 1604 and 1616, and its comic scenes may be partly by other writers. Its magnificent verse and portrait of an overreaching intellect made it a landmark of English tragedy, and the Faust legend was taken up again by Goethe and Thomas Mann.

title: Romeo and Juliet
creator: William Shakespeare
location: London; first printed 1597 (quarto)
description: Romeo and Juliet is an early tragedy, based mainly on Arthur Brooke's poem The Tragicall Historye of Romeus and Juliet (1562), itself derived from Italian novellas. In Verona the Montagues and Capulets are locked in an ancient feud. Romeo, a Montague, gatecrashes a Capulet feast and falls in love with Juliet, the Capulet daughter; they meet at her balcony and are secretly married the next day by Friar Laurence. When Juliet's cousin Tybalt kills Romeo's friend Mercutio, Romeo kills Tybalt and is banished. To escape a forced marriage, Juliet takes a potion that simulates death, but the message explaining the plan fails to reach Romeo, who poisons himself at her tomb; Juliet wakes and stabs herself. The play's lyrical verse, including a sonnet shared by the lovers at their first meeting, and its mixture of comedy and tragedy made it one of Shakespeare's most popular works. It has inspired operas, Prokofiev's ballet, West Side Story and many films.

title: A Midsummer Night's Dream
creator: William Shakespeare
location: London; first printed 1600 (quarto)
description: A Midsummer Night's Dream interweaves several plots around the wedding of Theseus, duke of Athens, and the Amazon queen Hippolyta. Two pairs of young lovers flee into a wood, where Oberon, king of the fairies, quarrelling with his queen Titania, orders the mischievous Puck to use a love potion. Puck's mistakes set the lovers chasing the wrong partners, while Titania, under the same spell, falls in love with the weaver Bottom, whose head Puck has turned into an ass's. Bottom and his fellow craftsmen are rehearsing a play, Pyramus and Thisbe, for the duke's wedding, and their hilariously inept performance ends the play. Shakespeare drew on Ovid, Chaucer and English folklore but invented the overall design himself. The play's blend of poetry, farce and enchantment, and its reflections on love, imagination and theatre, have made it one of his most performed comedies, inspiring Mendelssohn's incidental music and Britten's opera.

title: Hamlet
creator: William Shakespeare
location: London, Globe Theatre; first printed 1603 (quarto)
description: Hamlet, Prince of Denmark, is Shakespeare's longest play and probably the most famous play in the world. Returning from university to the Danish court at Elsinore, Hamlet finds his father dead and his mother Gertrude remarried to his uncle Claudius, the new king. His father's ghost reveals that Claudius murdered him and demands revenge. Hamlet feigns madness, rejects Ophelia, whom he loves, stages a play to test the king's guilt, and mistakenly kills Ophelia's father Polonius, after which Ophelia goes mad and drowns. Claudius sends Hamlet to England to be killed, but he escapes and returns. In a final fencing match arranged by Claudius with Ophelia's brother Laertes, Gertrude, Laertes, Claudius and Hamlet all die. The play survives in three early versions that differ significantly. Its soliloquies, above all To be or not to be, and its hero's searching, delaying intelligence have made it a central text for ideas about consciousness and modern selfhood.

title: Twelfth Night
creator: William Shakespeare
location: First recorded performance at Middle Temple Hall, London, February 1602; printed in the First Folio, 1623
description: Twelfth Night, or What You Will takes its title from the last night of the Christmas festivities, a time of revelry and misrule. Shipwrecked on the coast of Illyria and believing her twin brother Sebastian drowned, Viola disguises herself as a page, Cesario, and enters the service of Duke Orsino, whom she comes to love. Orsino sends her to woo the countess Olivia, who falls in love with Cesario. In a comic subplot, Olivia's riotous uncle Sir Toby Belch, the foolish Sir Andrew Aguecheek and the maid Maria trick her pompous steward Malvolio into believing that Olivia loves him, and he is locked up as mad. The arrival of Sebastian, who is mistaken for Cesario and promptly married by Olivia, resolves the confusion. The play's songs, sung by the fool Feste, and its bittersweet mixture of festivity and melancholy make it one of the finest of Shakespeare's comedies. Its play with gender and disguise has given it new life in modern productions.

title: Othello
creator: William Shakespeare
location: First recorded performance at Whitehall, London, 1604; first printed 1622 (quarto)
description: Othello, the Moor of Venice is based on a story in Giraldi Cinthio's collection Hecatommithi (1565). Othello, a black general in the service of Venice, has secretly married Desdemona, daughter of a senator. His ensign Iago, resentful at being passed over for promotion in favour of Cassio and nursing vague suspicions, sets out to destroy him. On Cyprus, where Othello has been sent to defend the island against the Turks, Iago gets Cassio drunk and disgraced, then insinuates that Desdemona is having an affair with him, using a handkerchief she has dropped as false proof. Consumed by jealousy, Othello smothers Desdemona in her bed. When Iago's wife Emilia reveals the truth, Othello kills himself. With its tight construction and focus on a few characters, the play is the most domestic of Shakespeare's tragedies. Iago's motiveless malignity, as Coleridge called it, and the play's treatment of race have made it a subject of intense critical and theatrical attention. Verdi based his opera Otello on it.

title: Don Quixote
creator: Miguel de Cervantes
location: Madrid, printed by Juan de la Cuesta
description: The Ingenious Gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha was published in two parts, in 1605 and 1615. Alonso Quixano, a minor gentleman of La Mancha, reads so many books of chivalry that he loses his wits, renames himself Don Quixote, takes an old nag called Rocinante and a peasant woman he imagines as his lady Dulcinea, and sets out to right wrongs. With his down-to-earth squire Sancho Panza he attacks windmills he takes for giants, frees galley slaves and suffers beatings and humiliations. In the second part, written after a spurious sequel by another author appeared, the characters have read the first part and are recognised wherever they go, and a duke and duchess stage elaborate pranks on them. Finally defeated, Don Quixote returns home, recovers his sanity and dies. The novel's play of illusion and reality, its self-awareness as fiction and the evolving friendship of knight and squire made it a model for the European novel. It is one of the most translated books in the world.

title: King Lear
creator: William Shakespeare
location: Performed at Whitehall before James I, December 1606; first printed 1608 (quarto)
description: King Lear draws on the legend of a pre-Christian British king recorded by Geoffrey of Monmouth and dramatised in an earlier anonymous play. The aged Lear decides to divide his kingdom among his three daughters according to how much they say they love him. Goneril and Regan flatter him extravagantly; the youngest, Cordelia, refuses to, and he disinherits her. His elder daughters then strip him of his followers and shut him out into a storm, where he goes mad on the heath, accompanied by his Fool and the disguised Earl of Kent. In a parallel plot, the Earl of Gloucester is deceived by his illegitimate son Edmund against his loyal son Edgar and is blinded. Cordelia returns with a French army but is defeated and hanged, and Lear dies with her body in his arms. The play survives in two different versions, the 1608 quarto and the 1623 Folio. Once thought too bleak to stage without a happy ending, it is now often considered Shakespeare's greatest tragedy.

title: Macbeth
creator: William Shakespeare
location: London; first printed in the First Folio, 1623
description: Macbeth, Shakespeare's shortest tragedy, is based loosely on Holinshed's Chronicles and was probably written with James I, the patron of Shakespeare's company and a descendant of Banquo, in mind. Returning victorious from battle, the Scottish generals Macbeth and Banquo meet three witches, who hail Macbeth as future king and Banquo as the father of kings. Urged on by Lady Macbeth, Macbeth murders King Duncan as he sleeps in their castle and takes the throne. To secure it he has Banquo killed and slaughters the family of the nobleman Macduff. Haunted by Banquo's ghost, Macbeth becomes a bloody tyrant, while Lady Macbeth, sleepwalking, tries to wash invisible blood from her hands and dies. Trusting the witches' further riddling prophecies, Macbeth is killed by Macduff. The play's dark atmosphere, its imagery of blood, night and sleep, and its exploration of ambition and guilt make it one of the most powerful of the tragedies. Theatrical superstition holds that its name should not be spoken in a theatre.

title: Sonnets
creator: William Shakespeare
location: London, published by Thomas Thorpe
description: Shake-speares Sonnets was published in 1609 by Thomas Thorpe, with a mysterious dedication to Mr. W. H. as their only begetter; whether Shakespeare authorised the publication is debated. The 154 poems use the English sonnet form of three quatrains and a couplet, which became known as the Shakespearean sonnet. The first 126 are mostly addressed to a beautiful young man, urging him first to marry and have children and then promising him immortality in verse; others are addressed to a dark lady, the poet's mistress, with frank and bitter sexuality, and several concern a rival poet. Attempts to identify these figures with real people have filled many books without agreement. The sonnets explore love, desire, betrayal, ageing and time with unrivalled verbal richness, and poems such as Shall I compare thee to a summer's day? and Let me not to the marriage of true minds are among the most famous in English.

title: The Tempest
creator: William Shakespeare
location: Performed at Whitehall, November 1611; printed as the first play in the First Folio, 1623
description: The Tempest is probably the last play Shakespeare wrote alone. Prospero, the rightful duke of Milan, was overthrown by his brother Antonio and set adrift with his young daughter Miranda; they reached an island where Prospero, a master of magic, freed the spirit Ariel and enslaved the native Caliban. Twelve years later, a ship carrying Antonio, Alonso, king of Naples, and his son Ferdinand passes, and Prospero conjures a storm that wrecks them on the island. Through Ariel he separates the survivors, brings Miranda and Ferdinand together, foils a plot by Caliban and two drunken servants, and finally confronts his enemies, choosing forgiveness over revenge. He then breaks his staff, frees Ariel and asks the audience to set him free. Drawing on accounts of a shipwreck in Bermuda in 1609 and on Montaigne, the play has often been read as Shakespeare's farewell to the stage and, since the twentieth century, as a reflection on colonialism through the figure of Caliban.

title: Fuenteovejuna
creator: Lope de Vega
location: Madrid, in the Dozena parte of Lope's comedias
description: Fuenteovejuna is based on a real event of 1476, when the inhabitants of a village in Andalusia killed the commander of the military Order of Calatrava, Fernán Gómez de Guzmán. In Lope's play the commander abuses the villagers and assaults their women, and when he abducts the young Laurencia on her wedding day, she rouses the village to revolt with a fiery speech shaming the men. The villagers storm his house and kill him. The Catholic Monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella send a judge to find the guilty, but even under torture every villager, from children to old men, answers only that Fuenteovejuna did it. Unable to punish the whole town, the king pardons them. The play combines a love story, a political plot and a vision of collective dignity and loyalty to the crown. Long neglected, it was revived in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries as a drama of popular revolt, and staged in Soviet Russia and by Lorca's touring theatre in Republican Spain.

title: Holy Sonnets
creator: John Donne
location: London, in Poems (posthumous, 1633)
description: The Holy Sonnets, also called the Divine Meditations, are nineteen sonnets mostly written around 1609–1610, during a period of illness, poverty and religious crisis before Donne's ordination. They circulated in manuscript and were first printed in his posthumous Poems of 1633, in a sequence and number that differ between manuscripts. The poems bring the urgent, dramatic voice and intellectual daring of Donne's love poetry to devotion: the speaker contemplates the last judgement, confronts his sin and fear of damnation, and addresses God in startling terms. Death be not proud defies death itself, and Batter my heart, three-personed God asks God to overthrow and ravish the speaker so that he may be free. The sonnets show the influence of Ignatian meditation and the tensions between Donne's Catholic upbringing and his Anglican faith. Benjamin Britten set nine of them to music, and they are among the finest religious poems in English.

title: Life Is a Dream
creator: Pedro Calderón de la Barca
location: Madrid, in the first part of Calderón's comedias, 1636
description: Life Is a Dream (La vida es sueño) is Calderón's most celebrated play. King Basilio of Poland, an astrologer, has read in the stars that his son Segismundo will become a tyrant, and has kept him chained in a tower since birth. As an experiment, Basilio has Segismundo drugged and brought to court. Waking as a prince, Segismundo behaves violently, throwing a servant from a balcony, and is drugged again and returned to the tower, where he is told it was all a dream. Released by rebellious soldiers who want him as king, he resolves to act well whether he is dreaming or not, defeats his father and pardons him. A second plot follows Rosaura, a woman disguised as a man who seeks to restore her honour. The play's meditations on free will, fate, illusion and the nature of reality, culminating in Segismundo's famous soliloquy, made it a major work of European drama, admired by the German Romantics and constantly revived.

title: The Misanthrope
creator: Molière (Jean-Baptiste Poquelin)
location: Palais-Royal theatre, Paris
description: The Misanthrope is often considered Molière's most profound comedy. Alceste refuses all compromise with the politeness and flattery of fashionable society and insists on telling the truth whatever the cost; his friend Philinte argues that one must accept human nature and be tolerant. Yet Alceste loves Célimène, a witty young widow who delights in society, gossip and admirers. He offends a courtier by criticising his sonnet, which leads to a lawsuit, and loses another case that he refuses to fight by the usual means. When Célimène's letters mocking all her suitors are revealed, they abandon her; she is willing to marry Alceste but not to leave the world for a solitary life with him, and he departs alone. Written in alexandrine verse, the play has little action and much conversation, and its ending is far from simple comedy. Rousseau criticised it for mocking a virtuous man, and audiences still debate whether Alceste is admirable or ridiculous.

title: Paradise Lost
creator: John Milton
location: London, published by Samuel Simmons (10 books; revised in 12 books, 1674)
description: Paradise Lost was dictated by the blind Milton in the years around the Restoration and published in 1667 in ten books, revised into twelve in 1674. In more than ten thousand lines of blank verse, it begins in medias res with Satan and the rebel angels cast into Hell after their failed war in Heaven. Satan rallies them, escapes through Chaos and reaches the newly created world, where he tempts Eve, in the form of a serpent, to eat the forbidden fruit; Adam eats too, out of love for her. The archangel Raphael tells Adam of the war in Heaven and the creation, and Michael shows him the future history of humanity up to Christ's redemption before the couple leave Eden hand in hand. Milton's grand, Latinate verse and the charismatic figure of Satan have provoked debate ever since, from Blake and Shelley's view of Satan as the true hero to modern readings of its politics and gender. It is the greatest epic poem in English.

title: Tartuffe
creator: Molière (Jean-Baptiste Poquelin)
location: Versailles (first version, 1664); Palais-Royal theatre, Paris (1669)
description: Tartuffe, or the Impostor caused the greatest scandal of Molière's career. A first three-act version was performed for Louis XIV at Versailles in 1664, but the Archbishop of Paris and the devout party at court were outraged, and the play was banned. Molière revised it twice and was finally allowed to stage the five-act version in 1669, when it was a triumph. The wealthy Orgon has taken into his house Tartuffe, whom he believes a holy man, and is so infatuated that he plans to give him his daughter's hand and signs over his property. His wife Elmire exposes Tartuffe by letting Orgon hide under a table while the hypocrite tries to seduce her. Tartuffe then uses the deed and compromising papers to evict the family and denounce Orgon, but a royal officer arrives to arrest the impostor in the name of the all-seeing king. Written in alexandrine couplets, the play is Molière's sharpest attack on religious hypocrisy, and Tartuffe's name became a word for a hypocrite.

title: Phèdre
creator: Jean Racine
location: Hôtel de Bourgogne, Paris
description: Phèdre, first performed in Paris on 1 January 1677, is based on Euripides's Hippolytus and Seneca's Phaedra. Phèdre, wife of Theseus, king of Athens, has long hidden her desperate love for her stepson Hippolyte. When news arrives that Theseus is dead, her nurse Oenone persuades her to confess it, and Hippolyte, who loves the captive princess Aricie, recoils in horror. Theseus then returns alive. To save her mistress, Oenone accuses Hippolyte of attempting to seduce Phèdre, and Theseus curses his son and calls on Neptune to destroy him; Hippolyte is killed by a sea monster that frightens his horses. Phèdre, tortured by guilt and jealousy, takes poison and confesses the truth before dying. Racine presents passion as a fatal force that the will cannot master, in alexandrine verse of exceptional beauty. A rival play on the same subject was staged at the same time by Racine's enemies, and the controversy may have contributed to his withdrawal from the theatre. Phèdre remains the summit of French classical tragedy and one of the great roles for actresses.

title: Robinson Crusoe
creator: Daniel Defoe
location: London, published by William Taylor
description: The Life and Strange Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe was published in April 1719 as if it were the true autobiography of its hero, with no author's name on the title page. Crusoe, a young man from York, defies his father to go to sea, is captured by pirates, escapes, becomes a plantation owner in Brazil and, on a slave-trading voyage, is shipwrecked on an uninhabited island off the coast of South America. Salvaging tools and provisions from the wreck, he builds a shelter, keeps goats, grows grain, makes pottery and keeps a journal, while gradually finding religious faith. After many years he rescues a native man from cannibals, names him Friday and makes him his servant, and eventually he is rescued by an English ship. Partly inspired by the experiences of the castaway Alexander Selkirk, the novel's realistic detail made it a sensation. It has been read as a myth of economic individualism and, more recently, of colonialism, and it inspired a whole genre of castaway stories.

title: Gulliver's Travels
creator: Jonathan Swift
location: London, published by Benjamin Motte
description: Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World, by Lemuel Gulliver was published anonymously in 1726, with passages softened by the publisher for fear of prosecution; a corrected edition appeared in 1735. In four voyages the ship's surgeon Gulliver is shipwrecked in Lilliput, where people are six inches tall and wage war over which end to break an egg; abandoned in Brobdingnag, where giants find him a curiosity and the king judges Europeans a pernicious race of odious vermin; visits the flying island of Laputa and its absurd scientists; and finally reaches the land of the Houyhnhnms, wise horses who rule over brutish human creatures called Yahoos. Gulliver returns home unable to bear the company of his own family. Swift satirised politics, science, war and human pride with deadpan precision. Though shortened versions of the first two voyages became children's classics, the full book is one of the darkest and most influential satires in literature.

title: A Modest Proposal
creator: Jonathan Swift
location: Dublin, published as a pamphlet
description: A Modest Proposal for Preventing the Children of Poor People from Being a Burthen to Their Parents or Country was published anonymously in Dublin in 1729, after years of famine and English economic restrictions on Ireland. In the reasonable, statistical voice of a public-spirited economist, the author observes the misery of beggar women and their children and proposes that poor Irish parents should sell their year-old infants to be eaten by the wealthy, calculating the costs and benefits and suggesting recipes. Only near the end does he dismiss, as impractical, the real remedies, such as taxing absentee landlords and buying Irish goods, that Swift had urged elsewhere. The essay attacks the dehumanising language of political economy, English exploitation and Irish landlords, and it is the most famous example of sustained irony in English. A modest proposal has become a standard phrase for satirical suggestions.

title: Candide
creator: Voltaire (François-Marie Arouet)
location: Geneva, published by Gabriel Cramer (simultaneously in several cities)
description: Candide, or Optimism was published anonymously in January 1759 and immediately banned in several places; it became one of the bestsellers of the century. Candide is expelled from a German baron's castle for kissing his daughter Cunégonde and goes through a breathless series of catastrophes: forced military service, the Lisbon earthquake of 1755, the Inquisition, shipwreck, the mythical land of Eldorado and slavery in Surinam, while his tutor Pangloss insists that everything is for the best. Characters die and reappear, and the reunited companions settle on a small farm near Constantinople, where Candide concludes that we must cultivate our garden. Voltaire's target was the philosophical optimism associated with Leibniz and Pope, but the tale also mocks religion, war, colonialism and aristocratic pride. Its speed, irony and comic cruelty make it the most famous of the Enlightenment's philosophical tales, and it inspired Bernstein's operetta.

title: Tristram Shandy
creator: Laurence Sterne
location: York (vols 1–2) and London
description: The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman appeared in nine volumes between 1759 and 1767. Its narrator, Tristram, sets out to tell his life and opinions but begins with the moment of his conception, interrupted by his mother's question about winding the clock, and digresses so constantly that he is not born until volume three. Instead the book is filled with his eccentric father Walter, who has theories about names and noses; his uncle Toby, a gentle old soldier obsessed with re-creating the sieges of the War of the Spanish Succession on a bowling green; Toby's servant Corporal Trim; and the parson Yorick. Sterne plays with the printed page: a black page mourns Yorick, a marbled page appears as an emblem, chapters are missing, and diagrams show the wanderings of the plot. Wildly popular and condemned by Samuel Johnson, who predicted it would not last, the novel was later recognised as a precursor of Modernist and postmodern fiction.

title: Julie, or the New Heloise
creator: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
location: Amsterdam, published by Marc-Michel Rey
description: Julie, or the New Heloise takes its subtitle from the medieval lovers Abelard and Heloise. Told in letters, it begins in a village at the foot of the Alps on Lake Geneva, where the young tutor Saint-Preux and his aristocratic pupil Julie d'Étange fall in love and become lovers. Her father forbids the match on grounds of class, and Julie obeys him by marrying the older, rational, atheist Baron de Wolmar. Years later Wolmar invites Saint-Preux to live with them at their estate of Clarens, which Rousseau presents as a model community of virtue and natural order, until Julie dies after rescuing her child from the lake, her last letter confessing that she has never stopped loving Saint-Preux. With its intense feeling, moral reflection and descriptions of mountain scenery, the novel ran through dozens of editions and provoked a flood of letters from readers. It was a major source of the cult of sensibility and of Romantic attitudes to nature and love.

title: The Sorrows of Young Werther
creator: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
location: Leipzig, published by Weygand
description: The Sorrows of Young Werther was written in a few weeks and drew on Goethe's own infatuation with Charlotte Buff, who was engaged to his friend Johann Christian Kestner, and on the suicide of an acquaintance, Karl Wilhelm Jerusalem. The novel consists mainly of letters from Werther, a young artist, to his friend Wilhelm. In a country town he meets Lotte and falls passionately in love with her, though she is engaged and then married to the decent, sober Albert. Werther's letters chart his rapture in nature and in Homer and Ossian, his frustration with social conventions and his growing despair, until he borrows Albert's pistols and shoots himself. The book made Goethe famous throughout Europe at twenty-five, set a fashion for Werther's blue coat and yellow waistcoat, and was blamed for imitative suicides. It is the central novel of the Sturm und Drang, and Napoleon claimed to have read it seven times.

title: Songs of Innocence and of Experience
creator: William Blake
location: London; relief-etched, printed and hand-coloured by Blake and his wife
description: Blake printed Songs of Innocence in 1789 and combined it with Songs of Experience in 1794, with the subtitle Shewing the Two Contrary States of the Human Soul. Each poem was etched on copper together with its illustration and decoration using a relief technique Blake invented, then printed and coloured by hand by him and his wife Catherine, so that every copy differs; only a few dozen were made. Many poems are paired: The Lamb with The Tyger, the Innocent Chimney Sweeper with the Experienced one, Holy Thursday with its bitter counterpart. In simple forms drawn from hymns and nursery rhymes, the songs move from the joy and trust of childhood to a world of repression, poverty, child labour and organised religion, and poems such as London expose the mind-forged manacles of society. Little known in Blake's lifetime, the Songs are now among the most famous poems in English and are treasured as works of visual art.

title: Lyrical Ballads
creator: William Wordsworth
location: Bristol, published by Joseph Cottle; enlarged edition with Preface, London 1800
description: Lyrical Ballads, with a Few Other Poems was published anonymously in 1798, the fruit of the close collaboration of Wordsworth and Coleridge in Somerset. According to Coleridge's later account, he was to write poems of the supernatural made believable, while Wordsworth would give the charm of novelty to things of every day. Coleridge contributed The Rime of the Ancient Mariner and three other pieces, Wordsworth the rest, including poems about rural poor people, children and outcasts such as We Are Seven, Simon Lee and The Thorn, and the meditative Lines Written a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey. The second edition of 1800, in two volumes under Wordsworth's name, added his Preface, which argued for poetry in the real language of men and defined it as the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings. The book received mixed reviews, but it is now regarded as the founding document of English Romantic poetry.

title: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
creator: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
location: Bristol, in Lyrical Ballads; revised with marginal glosses in Sibylline Leaves, 1817
description: The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere, as it was spelled in its first version, opened Lyrical Ballads in 1798; Coleridge modernised its language in later editions and in 1817 added a prose gloss in the margin, written in the voice of an antiquarian scholar. An old mariner stops a young man on his way to a wedding and holds him with his glittering eye while he tells his story. His ship was driven by storms towards the South Pole, where an albatross appeared and led it out of the ice, and the mariner shot it with his crossbow. The ship is becalmed under a burning sun, the crew die of thirst after a ghostly ship carrying Death and Life-in-Death passes, and the mariner is released from the curse only when he blesses the sea creatures in his heart. He must wander the earth telling his tale. Its vivid images and haunting music made it one of the best-known poems in English, and its phrases, such as an albatross around one's neck, became proverbial. Gustave Doré illustrated it in 1876.

title: Faust
creator: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
location: Tübingen, published by Cotta (Part One); Part Two published posthumously, 1832
description: Goethe worked on Faust for about sixty years, from the early Urfaust of the 1770s to the completion of the second part shortly before his death. In a Prologue in Heaven, Mephistopheles wagers with the Lord that he can lead the striving scholar Faust astray. Faust, despairing of knowledge, makes a pact with the devil: if ever he should be so content with a moment as to ask it to stay, he will forfeit his soul. Part One centres on Faust's seduction of the young Gretchen, who kills their child and is executed, but is saved by heaven. Part Two, vast and allegorical, takes Faust through the imperial court, classical antiquity and a union with Helen of Troy, to his final work reclaiming land from the sea; at his death he is carried to heaven by angels. Mixing verse forms, tragedy, comedy and philosophy, the work is the summit of German literature. It inspired Berlioz, Gounod, Liszt, Mahler and Thomas Mann, and gave the adjective Faustian to many languages.

title: Pride and Prejudice
creator: Jane Austen
location: London, published by Thomas Egerton
description: Pride and Prejudice was begun in 1796 as First Impressions, rejected by a publisher unread and revised before its anonymous publication in 1813 by the author of Sense and Sensibility. Mr and Mrs Bennet of Longbourn have five daughters and no son, so their estate will pass to a cousin, the absurd clergyman Mr Collins, and Mrs Bennet is desperate to marry them off. When the wealthy Mr Bingley rents a nearby house, he falls for the eldest, Jane, while his friend Mr Darcy offends the second daughter, Elizabeth, by his arrogance. Elizabeth's prejudice is fed by the charming officer Wickham, and she refuses Darcy's first, condescending proposal. His letter explaining his conduct, a visit to his estate of Pemberley and his help in rescuing her sister Lydia from disgrace after she elopes with Wickham lead each to recognise their faults. The novel's dialogue, ironic narration and famous opening sentence have made it one of the most loved novels in English, the source of countless adaptations.

title: Emma
creator: Jane Austen
location: London, published by John Murray
description: Emma was published in December 1815, dedicated by permission to the Prince Regent. Austen said she was creating a heroine whom no one but herself would much like. Emma Woodhouse lives with her valetudinarian father in the village of Highbury and, after the marriage of her governess, takes up matchmaking. She persuades her protégée Harriet Smith to reject a farmer who loves her in hopes of the vicar Mr Elton, who in fact wants to marry Emma; she flirts with the charming Frank Churchill without realising he is secretly engaged to the accomplished Jane Fairfax; and she humiliates the poor, garrulous Miss Bates at a picnic on Box Hill, for which her old friend Mr Knightley rebukes her. When Harriet confides that she hopes to marry Mr Knightley, Emma realises that she loves him herself. Built on misunderstandings that readers share with the heroine, Emma is a masterpiece of irony and of free indirect style, and many critics consider it Austen's most accomplished novel. It inspired the film Clueless.

title: Kubla Khan
creator: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
location: London, published by John Murray with Christabel and The Pains of Sleep
description: Kubla Khan, or A Vision in a Dream: A Fragment was published in 1816 at Byron's urging, nearly twenty years after its composition. In a preface Coleridge explained that in 1797, in a farmhouse near Porlock, he had fallen asleep after taking an anodyne, a reference to opium, while reading about the Mongol emperor Kublai Khan in Purchas's Pilgrimage, and composed two or three hundred lines in his sleep. On waking he began to write them down, but was interrupted by a person on business from Porlock, and when he returned the vision had vanished. The fifty-four lines describe the pleasure-dome of Xanadu, the sacred river Alph running through caverns measureless to man and an Abyssinian maid with a dulcimer, before turning to the poet who could rebuild the dome in song. Scholars debate how far the preface is literally true. The poem's incantatory music has made it one of the most famous of Romantic poems and a byword for inspiration.

title: Frankenstein
creator: Mary Shelley
location: London, published anonymously by Lackington, Hughes, Harding, Mavor & Jones
description: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus was published anonymously in three volumes in 1818, with a preface by Percy Shelley; a revised edition of 1831 bore Mary Shelley's name and a famous introduction describing its origin in a ghost-story contest with Byron at the Villa Diodati near Geneva in 1816. The novel is told in nested narratives. The Arctic explorer Robert Walton writes to his sister of rescuing Victor Frankenstein, a Genevan who, as a student at Ingolstadt, discovered the secret of life and assembled a creature from parts of corpses. Horrified by its appearance, he fled. The creature, abandoned and rejected by everyone he meets, educates himself by secretly watching a family and reading Paradise Lost, then, in his own eloquent narrative, demands a mate; when Victor destroys the female he was making, the creature kills his friend and his bride. Victor pursues him to the Arctic and dies. The novel fused the Gothic with questions about science, responsibility and alienation, and it is often called the first work of science fiction.

title: Don Juan
creator: Lord Byron (George Gordon Byron)
location: London, published by John Murray (cantos 1–5) and John Hunt
description: Don Juan was published in instalments from 1819 until 1824, when Byron died having completed sixteen cantos and part of a seventeenth. Written in ottava rima, an Italian stanza of eight lines rhyming abababcc that Byron used for comic effect, it inverts the legend of the great seducer: Juan is a handsome, rather passive young man more often pursued than pursuing. Sent abroad after an affair with a married woman in Seville, he is shipwrecked, loved by the pirate's daughter Haidée on a Greek island, sold as a slave in Constantinople, fights at the siege of Ismail, becomes a favourite of Catherine the Great and finally visits English country-house society. Around the story, the narrator digresses freely on politics, poetry, love, his contemporaries and himself, mocking Wordsworth, Southey and Wellington. The poem's frankness scandalised its first readers, and Murray stopped publishing it, but it is now regarded as Byron's masterpiece and one of the great comic poems in English.

title: Ode to a Nightingale
creator: John Keats
location: Annals of the Fine Arts, July 1819; collected in Lamia, Isabella, The Eve of St Agnes, and Other Poems, 1820
description: Ode to a Nightingale was written in May 1819 at Wentworth Place in Hampstead, where Keats was living with his friend Charles Brown, who recalled that a nightingale had built its nest nearby and that Keats sat under a plum tree in the garden one morning and wrote the poem on scraps of paper. It is one of the group of great odes Keats composed that spring, along with those on a Grecian urn, melancholy, indolence and Psyche. In eight ten-line stanzas, the speaker, aching and numb, hears the bird's song and longs to fade away with it, leaving behind the weariness, the fever and the fret of a world where youth grows pale and dies, a reference to his brother Tom's recent death from tuberculosis. He imagines wine and then poetry carrying him to the bird, considers that it would be rich to die, and contrasts his mortality with the immortal song, before the vision fades. The ode's rich sensuous imagery and its meditation on art, beauty and death make it one of the most celebrated poems in English.

title: Prometheus Unbound
creator: Percy Bysshe Shelley
location: London, published by Charles and James Ollier
description: Prometheus Unbound, a Lyrical Drama in Four Acts was written in Italy in 1818–19 and published in 1820. Aeschylus's lost sequel to Prometheus Bound apparently reconciled the Titan with Zeus; Shelley, rejecting what he called so feeble a catastrophe, made it a drama of liberation. Prometheus, chained to a precipice in the Caucasus for three thousand years, recalls and withdraws the curse he once laid on Jupiter, refusing hatred. His beloved Asia, guided by her sister Panthea, descends to the cave of Demogorgon, a mysterious primal power, and at the appointed hour Demogorgon dethrones Jupiter. Prometheus is freed by Hercules, and the last acts, in dazzling lyrical choruses, celebrate a renewed universe in which humanity is free, equal and governed by love. Shelley's preface explains his aim to familiarise readers with beautiful idealisms of moral excellence. The poem is the fullest expression of his radical political and philosophical hopes.

title: Notre-Dame de Paris (The Hunchback of Notre-Dame)
creator: Victor Hugo
location: Paris, published by Gosselin
description: Notre-Dame de Paris, known in English as The Hunchback of Notre-Dame, was published in 1831 and is set in Paris in 1482. The beautiful young Roma dancer Esmeralda attracts the obsessive desire of Claude Frollo, the austere archdeacon of Notre-Dame, who orders his deaf, deformed adopted son Quasimodo, the cathedral's bell-ringer, to abduct her. She is rescued by the handsome captain Phoebus, whom she loves. When Frollo stabs Phoebus out of jealousy, Esmeralda is accused of the crime and condemned. Quasimodo, who has come to love her, carries her into the cathedral to claim sanctuary, but she is eventually captured and hanged, and Quasimodo throws Frollo from the tower; years later two skeletons are found embraced in a charnel house. The novel is also a celebration of Gothic architecture, and its success helped spark a movement to preserve Notre-Dame and other medieval buildings, leading to the cathedral's restoration by Viollet-le-Duc. It has been adapted many times for stage and screen.

title: Eugene Onegin
creator: Alexander Pushkin
location: Saint Petersburg (serialised in chapters; complete edition 1833)
description: Eugene Onegin was published in chapters between 1825 and 1832 and as a complete book in 1833. It is written in a stanza of fourteen lines of iambic tetrameter with an intricate rhyme scheme that Pushkin invented, now called the Onegin stanza. Onegin, a jaded young aristocrat of Saint Petersburg, inherits a country estate, where he befriends the young Romantic poet Lensky, engaged to Olga Larina. Olga's sister Tatyana, a dreamy reader of novels, falls in love with Onegin and writes him a letter declaring it; he coldly lectures her. At Tatyana's name-day party, Onegin flirts with Olga out of boredom, Lensky challenges him to a duel and Onegin kills him. Years later Onegin meets Tatyana again in Saint Petersburg, married to a prince and the queen of society, and falls passionately in love with her, but she, though she still loves him, refuses to betray her husband. With its witty narrator, digressions and panorama of Russian life, Belinsky called it an encyclopaedia of Russian life. Tchaikovsky made it into an opera, and Nabokov produced a famous literal translation.

title: Père Goriot
creator: Honoré de Balzac
location: Paris, serialised in the Revue de Paris (1834–35), then published by Werdet
description: Le Père Goriot was serialised in 1834–35 and published as a book in 1835. It is set in 1819 in the Maison Vauquer, a dingy boarding house in the Latin Quarter that Balzac describes in famous detail. Among its residents are old Goriot, a retired vermicelli maker who has given his fortune to his two daughters, now married into high society and ashamed of him; Eugène de Rastignac, an ambitious law student from the provinces; and the mysterious Vautrin, who offers Rastignac a criminal shortcut to wealth and is later revealed as an escaped convict. Rastignac becomes the lover of one of Goriot's daughters and witnesses how both daughters exploit their father, who dies alone and destitute, attended only by Rastignac. At the end Rastignac looks down over Paris from the cemetery of Père Lachaise and challenges the city. This was the first novel in which Balzac systematically used recurring characters, and it became a cornerstone of La Comédie humaine. Rastignac's name became a byword for an ambitious young man.

title: The Bronze Horseman
creator: Alexander Pushkin
location: Saint Petersburg (published posthumously in a censored version, 1837)
description: The Bronze Horseman: A Petersburg Tale was written in 1833 at Boldino, but Nicholas I, acting as Pushkin's personal censor, demanded changes, and it was published only after the poet's death, in an altered version. It begins with a celebrated prologue in praise of Peter the Great and the city he founded on the marshes of the Neva. The story then follows Evgeny, a poor clerk who dreams of marrying his sweetheart Parasha. During the great flood of November 1824 he sits stranded on a marble lion facing Falconet's equestrian statue of Peter; when the waters recede he finds that Parasha's house and family have been swept away. Driven mad, he wanders the city and, one night, shakes his fist at the statue, which seems to come alive and gallop after him through the streets. His body is later found on a small island. The poem's conflict between the individual and the state, and its mythic vision of Saint Petersburg, made it one of the most influential works in Russian literature, echoed by Gogol, Dostoevsky, Bely and Mandelstam.

title: The Fall of the House of Usher
creator: Edgar Allan Poe
location: Burton's Gentleman's Magazine, Philadelphia (September 1839)
description: The Fall of the House of Usher was published in Burton's Gentleman's Magazine in 1839 and collected in Tales of the Grotesque and Arabesque the following year. The unnamed narrator is summoned to the decaying mansion of his boyhood friend Roderick Usher, which stands above a dark tarn and has a barely visible crack running down its front. Roderick, the last of his line, suffers from a morbid acuteness of the senses and dread, while his twin sister Madeline wastes away from a mysterious illness. When Madeline apparently dies, the two men entomb her in a vault beneath the house. During a storm days later, as the narrator reads aloud to calm Roderick, sounds from the story seem to echo through the house, and Madeline appears at the door, bloodied, having been buried alive; she falls on her brother and both die. The narrator flees as the house splits along its crack and sinks into the tarn. The tale is the classic example of Poe's theory of a single unified effect and a cornerstone of Gothic fiction.

title: Dead Souls
creator: Nikolai Gogol
location: Moscow
description: Dead Souls was published in 1842; the censor insisted on the title The Adventures of Chichikov, or Dead Souls, objecting that souls are immortal. Gogol called it a poem, imagining it as the first part of a trilogy modelled on Dante's Divine Comedy. Pavel Ivanovich Chichikov, a smooth former civil servant, arrives in a provincial town and visits the surrounding landowners with an odd proposal: to buy the serfs, called souls, who have died since the last census but still count as alive for tax purposes, so that he can mortgage them as property. His visits introduce a gallery of grotesque landowners, the sentimental Manilov, the suspicious widow Korobochka, the brawling Nozdryov, the bearlike Sobakevich and the miser Plyushkin. When rumours spread, Chichikov flees in his troika, and the narrator compares Russia itself to a speeding troika. Gogol wrote a second part but burned most of it shortly before his death. The novel's satire, digressions and comic exuberance made it a foundation of Russian prose.

title: The Overcoat
creator: Nikolai Gogol
location: Saint Petersburg, in Gogol's Collected Works
description: The Overcoat was published in 1842 in the third volume of Gogol's collected works. Akaky Akakievich Bashmachkin is a timid, elderly copying clerk in a Saint Petersburg government department, mocked by his colleagues and content only when copying documents. When his threadbare coat can no longer be patched, he saves for months, going without tea and candles, and orders a new overcoat from a one-eyed tailor. The coat transforms his life, and his colleagues throw a party in its honour, but on the way home he is robbed of it. His pleas to a pompous Very Important Person for help end in a humiliating scolding, and he dies of fever. His ghost then haunts the city, stealing overcoats, until it seizes that of the Important Person. Blending comedy, pathos and the fantastic, the story became a founding text of Russian realism and its sympathy for the little man; the remark that Russian writers all came out from under Gogol's overcoat is traditionally attributed to Dostoevsky.

title: A Christmas Carol
creator: Charles Dickens
location: London, published by Chapman & Hall (19 December 1843)
description: A Christmas Carol in Prose, Being a Ghost Story of Christmas was written in about six weeks in the autumn of 1843, partly in response to a government report on child labour, and published just before Christmas with illustrations by John Leech; its first edition sold out in days. Ebenezer Scrooge, a cold, grasping London moneylender, dismisses Christmas as humbug. On Christmas Eve he is visited by the ghost of his late partner Jacob Marley, bound in chains forged by his own greed, who warns him that three spirits will come. The Ghost of Christmas Past shows Scrooge his lonely childhood and lost love; the Ghost of Christmas Present shows him the poor but loving household of his clerk Bob Cratchit, whose son Tiny Tim is ill; and the silent Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come shows him his own unmourned death. Scrooge wakes on Christmas morning a changed man. The story did much to shape the modern celebration of Christmas as a festival of family and charity, and it has been adapted countless times.

title: The Raven
creator: Edgar Allan Poe
location: New York, Evening Mirror (29 January 1845)
description: The Raven was published in the New York Evening Mirror in January 1845 and was immediately reprinted across the United States, making Poe famous. On a bleak December midnight, a lonely scholar reads old books to forget his lost Lenore. A tapping at his window admits a raven, which perches on a bust of Pallas Athena above his door and answers his questions with one word, Nevermore. Amused at first, the narrator grows increasingly frantic as he asks whether there is comfort for his grief and whether he will be reunited with Lenore in heaven, and the poem ends with his soul trapped in the raven's shadow. Poe wrote a famous essay, The Philosophy of Composition (1846), claiming to have constructed the poem methodically to produce a single effect of melancholy, though how seriously he meant it is debated. Its incantatory trochaic rhythm, internal rhymes and refrain have made it one of the most famous American poems. Mallarmé translated it, and Manet and Doré illustrated it.

title: Jane Eyre
creator: Charlotte Brontë
location: London, published by Smith, Elder & Co. under the name Currer Bell
description: Jane Eyre: An Autobiography was published in October 1847 under the pseudonym Currer Bell and was an immediate success. Jane, an orphan, is mistreated by her aunt Mrs Reed and sent to Lowood, a harsh charity school where her friend Helen Burns dies of consumption. After years as a pupil and teacher, she becomes governess at Thornfield Hall to the ward of the brooding Mr Rochester. They fall in love, but at the altar it is revealed that Rochester is already married to Bertha Mason, a Creole woman from Jamaica whom he keeps locked in the attic because of her madness. Jane flees, nearly dies on the moors and is taken in by the clergyman St John Rivers, who asks her to marry him and go to India as a missionary. Hearing Rochester's voice calling her, she returns to find Thornfield burned, Bertha dead and Rochester blinded and maimed, and marries him. The novel's passionate first-person narrator and her demand for equality made it revolutionary. Jean Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea (1966) retold Bertha's story.

title: Wuthering Heights
creator: Emily Brontë
location: London, published by Thomas Cautley Newby under the name Ellis Bell
description: Wuthering Heights was published in December 1847 under the pseudonym Ellis Bell, together with Anne Brontë's Agnes Grey. Its story is told mainly by the tenant Lockwood, who visits the bleak farmhouse of Wuthering Heights in 1801, and by the housekeeper Nelly Dean, who recounts its history.
