Mr Earnshaw brings home a dark-skinned foundling, Heathcliff, who forms an intense bond with his daughter Catherine and is persecuted by her brother Hindley. Catherine marries the refined Edgar Linton of Thrushcross Grange, though she declares that she is Heathcliff. Heathcliff leaves, returns rich and takes revenge on both families, marrying Edgar's sister Isabella and gaining control of both houses, while Catherine dies after giving birth. Only in the second generation, with Catherine's daughter and Hindley's son, is the cycle broken, and Heathcliff dies longing to rejoin Catherine's ghost. Its violence and complex structure baffled early reviewers, but it is now regarded as one of the greatest novels in English.

title: The Prelude
creator: William Wordsworth
location: London, published posthumously by Edward Moxon
description: The Prelude, or Growth of a Poet's Mind was intended as an introduction to a vast philosophical poem, The Recluse, that Wordsworth never completed. He wrote a two-book version in 1798–99, a thirteen-book version addressed to Coleridge in 1805, and revised it for the rest of his life; it was published as The Prelude by his widow in 1850, months after his death. In blank verse, it traces his childhood in the Lake District, including famous spots of time such as stealing a boat at night, his years at Cambridge, a walking tour of the Alps, his residence in London and in France during the Revolution, his political disillusion and crisis, and his recovery through nature and the imagination, culminating in a vision on Mount Snowdon. The poem made the poet's own mental development into the subject of epic, and it is regarded as one of the masterpieces of English poetry. Modern editors often prefer the 1805 text to the more conservative revision of 1850.

title: The Scarlet Letter
creator: Nathaniel Hawthorne
location: Boston, published by Ticknor, Reed & Fields
description: The Scarlet Letter: A Romance was published in 1850 with a long introductory essay, The Custom-House, in which Hawthorne describes his work at the Salem custom house and claims to have found there the scarlet letter and the papers that inspired the story. Set in Boston in the 1640s, the novel opens with Hester Prynne standing on the scaffold with her infant daughter Pearl, condemned to wear a scarlet A on her breast for adultery. She refuses to name the father. Her long-absent husband, a scholar, arrives in disguise, calls himself Roger Chillingworth and sets out to discover her lover, who is the revered young minister Arthur Dimmesdale. Chillingworth torments Dimmesdale, whose hidden guilt destroys his health, until, after a sermon of unusual power, the minister mounts the scaffold with Hester and Pearl, confesses and dies. Hester, through quiet charity, transforms the meaning of the letter. The novel's symbolism, psychological depth and critique of Puritan intolerance made it one of the first classics of American literature.

title: David Copperfield
creator: Charles Dickens
location: London, published in monthly parts by Bradbury & Evans
description: The Personal History of David Copperfield was published in nineteen monthly instalments in 1849–50, illustrated by Hablot K. Browne (Phiz). Told in the first person, it follows David from his birth in Suffolk, after his father's death, through his happy early childhood with his mother and the devoted servant Peggotty, to the cruelty of his stepfather Mr Murdstone, who sends him at ten to work in a London warehouse, an episode drawn directly from Dickens's own experience. He runs away to his eccentric aunt Betsey Trotwood in Dover, is educated, works as a law clerk and becomes a writer. Along the way he meets some of Dickens's most famous characters: the debt-ridden optimist Mr Micawber, the scheming, falsely humble clerk Uriah Heep, the charming but destructive Steerforth and the steadfast Agnes Wickfield, whom he finally marries after the death of his childlike first wife Dora. Dickens called it his favourite child, and Tolstoy and Freud both admired it.

title: Moby-Dick
creator: Herman Melville
location: London (as The Whale, October 1851) and New York (November 1851)
description: Moby-Dick; or, The Whale was first published in London in October 1851 as The Whale, in an expurgated edition without its epilogue, and a month later in New York. It opens with one of literature's most famous lines, Call me Ishmael. Ishmael, a restless young man, signs on to the whaling ship Pequod at Nantucket with his friend Queequeg, a harpooner from the South Seas. Once at sea, the monomaniac Captain Ahab reveals that the voyage's purpose is to hunt the white sperm whale Moby Dick, which bit off his leg. The narrative mixes adventure with long chapters on whale biology, the techniques of whaling, the meaning of whiteness and much else, and passages written like scenes from a play. After a three-day chase, the whale destroys the Pequod, and only Ishmael survives, floating on Queequeg's coffin. Reviews were mixed and sales were poor, and Melville died almost forgotten. Rediscovered in the 1920s, the novel is now considered one of the greatest American books.

title: Bleak House
creator: Charles Dickens
location: London, published in monthly parts by Bradbury & Evans
description: Bleak House was published in twenty monthly parts in 1852–53. It opens with a famous description of fog over London and the Court of Chancery, where the inheritance case of Jarndyce and Jarndyce has dragged on for generations. Half the novel is narrated in the present tense by an omniscient voice and half by Esther Summerson, an orphan who becomes housekeeper to the kindly John Jarndyce at Bleak House, with his young wards Ada and Richard, whom the case gradually destroys. The proud Lady Dedlock harbours a secret, which the sinister lawyer Tulkinghorn sets out to discover, until he is murdered and Inspector Bucket, one of the first detectives in English fiction, investigates. The novel's huge cast ranges from the crossing sweeper Jo to the philanthropist Mrs Jellyby, and its satire of the law and of social neglect is savage. When the case is finally settled, the costs have consumed the whole estate. Many critics regard it as Dickens's greatest achievement.

title: Bartleby, the Scrivener
creator: Herman Melville
location: Putnam's Magazine, New York (November–December 1853)
description: Bartleby, the Scrivener: A Story of Wall-Street was published anonymously in two parts in Putnam's Magazine in 1853 and collected in The Piazza Tales in 1856. The narrator, an elderly lawyer, employs several copyists, or scriveners, in his Wall Street office, among them the eccentric Turkey and Nippers. He hires a new one, the pallid, quiet Bartleby, who at first copies prodigiously. Then, asked to check a copy, Bartleby replies that he would prefer not to, and gradually he declines to do anything at all, while refusing to leave the office, where he is discovered to be living. Baffled and moved, the lawyer moves his practice elsewhere; Bartleby is taken to the Tombs prison, where he refuses to eat and dies. The narrator later hears a rumour that Bartleby had worked in the Dead Letter Office. The story's mixture of comedy and despair, and Bartleby's passive resistance, have prompted endless interpretations and anticipate Kafka and the literature of the absurd.

title: Leaves of Grass
creator: Walt Whitman
location: Brooklyn, printed at the shop of Andrew and James Rome (self-published, 1855)
description: The first edition of Leaves of Grass was published by Whitman himself in Brooklyn in July 1855: twelve untitled poems and a long prose preface, with an engraving of the poet in workman's clothes and no author's name on the title page. The opening poem, later called Song of Myself, announces a self that contains multitudes and embraces all people and things. Emerson wrote to Whitman greeting him at the beginning of a great career, and Whitman printed the letter in the second edition. He went on revising and expanding the book for the rest of his life, adding sections such as Children of Adam and Calamus, on sexual love and comradeship between men, and Drum-Taps, on the Civil War, with its elegies for Lincoln, When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd and O Captain! My Captain! The final deathbed edition of 1891–92 contains nearly four hundred poems. The book's free verse, frank sexuality and democratic vision were scandalous, but it became the foundation of modern American poetry.

title: Madame Bovary
creator: Gustave Flaubert
location: Paris, serialised in the Revue de Paris (1856); published by Michel Lévy (1857)
description: Madame Bovary: Provincial Manners was serialised in the Revue de Paris in 1856, with cuts made by the editors; Flaubert and the publishers were then prosecuted for offending public morals and religion, and their acquittal in February 1857 made the book a sensation when it appeared in volume form that April. Emma Rouault, a farmer's daughter educated in a convent and fed on romantic novels, marries Charles Bovary, a dull, devoted country doctor, and quickly finds her life in the small towns of Tostes and Yonville unbearable. She has affairs, first with the landowner Rodolphe, who abandons her, and then with the young clerk Léon, and runs up enormous debts with the scheming merchant Lheureux. Facing ruin, she swallows arsenic and dies an agonising death. Flaubert spent five years on the novel, striving for impersonal narration and perfect style. Its use of free indirect discourse and ironic detail made it a model of the modern novel, and the word bovarysme came to describe a romantic dissatisfaction with reality.

title: Les Fleurs du mal
creator: Charles Baudelaire
location: Paris, published by Poulet-Malassis et de Broise
description: Les Fleurs du mal, The Flowers of Evil, was published in June 1857, and within weeks Baudelaire and his publishers were prosecuted for offending public morals. He was fined and six poems, mostly on lesbian love and erotic subjects, were banned from the book; the ban was lifted only in 1949. A second edition of 1861 added thirty-five poems, including the section Parisian Scenes, and a posthumous edition followed in 1868. The book opens with an address To the Reader, who is called hypocrite, my fellow, my brother, and is organised in sections including Spleen and Ideal, Wine, Flowers of Evil, Revolt and Death. In classical forms, especially the sonnet and the alexandrine, Baudelaire wrote about erotic love and disgust, ennui, the crowds and poor of modern Paris, intoxication and the longing for escape, in poems such as Correspondences, The Albatross, To a Passer-by and The Voyage. The collection is often seen as the beginning of modern poetry and a key source of Symbolism.

title: Great Expectations
creator: Charles Dickens
location: London, serialised weekly in All the Year Round
description: Great Expectations was serialised weekly in Dickens's magazine All the Year Round from December 1860 to August 1861. Philip Pirrip, called Pip, an orphan raised by his harsh sister and her gentle husband, the blacksmith Joe Gargery, on the Kent marshes, helps an escaped convict on Christmas Eve. He is then summoned to Satis House to play with Estella, the cold ward of Miss Havisham, a rich recluse who has stopped all the clocks and still wears her wedding dress since being jilted. When a lawyer announces that Pip has great expectations from an unknown benefactor, he goes to London to become a gentleman, grows ashamed of Joe, and assumes Miss Havisham is his patron, until the convict Magwitch returns from Australia and reveals that he is the source of Pip's fortune. Narrated by the older Pip, the novel is a moving study of snobbery, guilt and loyalty. Dickens rewrote the ending at the suggestion of the novelist Bulwer-Lytton to make it less bleak, and both versions survive.

title: Les Misérables
creator: Victor Hugo
location: Brussels, published by A. Lacroix, Verboeckhoven & Cie (simultaneously in Paris)
description: Les Misérables was largely written in exile on Guernsey and published in 1862 in five parts, one of the great publishing events of the century. Jean Valjean, released after nineteen years in the galleys for stealing a loaf of bread and trying to escape, is transformed by the mercy of a bishop who forgives his theft of silver. Under a new name he becomes a prosperous factory owner and mayor, but he is relentlessly hunted by Inspector Javert. He rescues Cosette, the child of the abandoned working woman Fantine, from the brutal Thénardiers and raises her as his own. In Paris, Cosette falls in love with the young Marius, who joins the republican insurrection of June 1832; Valjean carries the wounded Marius through the sewers to safety, and Javert, unable to reconcile mercy with law, drowns himself. Hugo filled the novel with long digressions on Waterloo, convents, slang and the sewers of Paris. Its passion for social justice made it one of the most popular novels ever written, and the stage musical has made it known worldwide.

title: Notes from Underground
creator: Fyodor Dostoevsky
location: Saint Petersburg, in the magazine Epoch (Epokha)
description: Notes from Underground was published in 1864 in Epoch, the journal Dostoevsky ran with his brother, in a year of personal loss. In the first part, Underground, an unnamed former official of forty, living in a squalid Saint Petersburg room, delivers a rambling, self-contradictory monologue against the utopian rationalism of writers such as Chernyshevsky, who believed humans would act in their own enlightened interest. He insists that people value their free will above happiness and will act against their interests simply to prove they are not piano keys, and he mocks the ideal of a crystal palace. In the second part, Apropos of the Wet Snow, he recalls episodes from his youth: his obsession with a soldier who brushed him aside, a disastrous dinner with old schoolmates and his cruelty to the young prostitute Liza, who offers him love. The work's unreliable, hyperconscious narrator anticipated the great novels to come and was read by Nietzsche and the existentialists as a key modern text.

title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
creator: Lewis Carroll (Charles Lutwidge Dodgson)
location: London, published by Macmillan, with illustrations by John Tenniel
description: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland began as a story Charles Dodgson told to the three Liddell sisters on a rowing trip from Oxford on 4 July 1862. He wrote it out as Alice's Adventures Under Ground, with his own illustrations, as a gift for Alice Liddell, and then expanded it for publication by Macmillan in 1865 with forty-two illustrations by the Punch cartoonist John Tenniel. The first printing was withdrawn because Tenniel was unhappy with its quality. Bored on a riverbank, Alice follows a White Rabbit with a pocket watch down a rabbit hole and finds herself growing and shrinking after eating and drinking, swimming in a pool of her own tears and meeting the Caterpillar, the Duchess, the Cheshire Cat, the Mad Hatter and March Hare at their tea party, and the Queen of Hearts, who demands that everyone's head be cut off. The book ends with a trial and Alice waking up. Its puns, parodies and logical absurdities revolutionised children's literature, and it has been translated into well over a hundred languages.

title: Crime and Punishment
creator: Fyodor Dostoevsky
location: Moscow, serialised in The Russian Messenger (Russkiy Vestnik)
description: Crime and Punishment was serialised in The Russian Messenger through 1866, written under great financial pressure. Rodion Raskolnikov, a former student living in a tiny room in Saint Petersburg, has developed the theory that extraordinary men, like Napoleon, have the right to transgress moral law for a higher purpose. He murders an old pawnbroker with an axe, and is forced to kill her gentle sister too when she walks in. Falling into fever, he is drawn into a cat-and-mouse game with the shrewd investigator Porfiry Petrovich, while his mother and sister arrive and the cynical Svidrigailov pursues his sister. He finds compassion in Sonya Marmeladova, a young woman forced into prostitution to support her family, who reads him the story of Lazarus and persuades him to confess. In the epilogue he is sent to Siberia, where Sonya follows him and a spiritual renewal begins. Told mostly from inside Raskolnikov's feverish mind, the novel is a psychological thriller and a profound study of guilt, pride and redemption.

title: Sentimental Education
creator: Gustave Flaubert
location: Paris, published by Michel Lévy
description: Sentimental Education: The Story of a Young Man was published in 1869, though its first idea went back to Flaubert's youthful love for an older married woman, Élisa Schlésinger. In 1840 the eighteen-year-old Frédéric Moreau, on a steamboat on the Seine, sees Madame Arnoux, wife of an art dealer, and falls in love with her for life. In Paris he studies law, inherits money, frequents artists, journalists, bankers and courtesans and has affairs, while his love for Madame Arnoux remains unconsummated. The Revolution of 1848 and Louis-Napoleon's coup pass through the novel almost incidentally, seen through the eyes of characters who are distracted or self-interested. Years later Frédéric and his friend Deslauriers conclude that the best moment of their lives was a youthful failure to visit a brothel. The novel's aimless hero, its irony and its refusal of dramatic climax baffled readers but were admired by Henry James, Proust and Kafka as a new kind of fiction.

title: War and Peace
creator: Leo Tolstoy
location: Moscow, serialised in part in The Russian Messenger (1865–67), then in book form
description: War and Peace was written over six years at Yasnaya Polyana and appeared first in part as a serial called The Year 1805, then in six volumes from 1867 to 1869. Spanning the years 1805 to 1820, it follows several aristocratic families, especially the Rostovs, Bolkonskys and Bezukhovs, through the wars against Napoleon. Pierre Bezukhov, an awkward illegitimate son who inherits an immense fortune, searches for meaning through freemasonry, marriage and captivity; Prince Andrei Bolkonsky seeks glory at Austerlitz and finds a different truth lying wounded under the sky; and the vivid, impulsive Natasha Rostova grows from girlhood to womanhood. Battles are described from the confused viewpoint of soldiers, and the great set pieces include Borodino and the French occupation and burning of Moscow. Tolstoy interrupts the story with essays arguing that history is made not by great men but by countless individual actions. With some 580 characters, it is one of the longest and most celebrated novels ever written.

title: Through the Looking-Glass
creator: Lewis Carroll (Charles Lutwidge Dodgson)
location: London, published by Macmillan, with illustrations by John Tenniel
description: Through the Looking-Glass, and What Alice Found There was published in December 1871 as a sequel to Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, again with illustrations by John Tenniel. Playing with her kitten on a winter evening, Alice climbs through the mirror over the fireplace into a reversed world where she must run fast to stay in the same place. The landscape is a giant chessboard, and Alice joins the game as a white pawn, advancing square by square to become a queen. On the way she reads the nonsense poem Jabberwocky in mirror writing, meets the Red Queen and White Queen, Tweedledum and Tweedledee, who recite The Walrus and the Carpenter, Humpty Dumpty, who explains the meanings of words, and the gentle White Knight. The book is more structured and melancholy than its predecessor, and introduced words such as chortle and galumph. Its play with logic, language and mirror reversal has fascinated logicians, physicists and philosophers as well as children.

title: Middlemarch
creator: George Eliot (Mary Ann Evans)
location: Edinburgh and London, published in eight parts by William Blackwood and Sons
description: Middlemarch: A Study of Provincial Life was published in eight parts in 1871–72 and is set in a fictional Midlands town between 1829 and 1832, the years leading up to the Great Reform Act. It interweaves several stories. Dorothea Brooke, an ardent young woman longing to do good, marries the elderly scholar Edward Casaubon, whose life's work, a key to all mythologies, proves sterile, and his jealous will tries to prevent her from marrying his young cousin Will Ladislaw. The ambitious new doctor Tertius Lydgate, hoping to reform medicine, is drawn into debt by his marriage to the beautiful, selfish Rosamond Vincy. Rosamond's brother Fred courts Mary Garth, and the banker Bulstrode's hidden past ruins him. Eliot's narrator reflects with wisdom and irony on how lives are shaped by social circumstance and small choices, ending with a celebrated tribute to those who live faithfully a hidden life. Virginia Woolf called it one of the few English novels written for grown-up people, and it is often named the greatest English novel.

title: A Season in Hell
creator: Arthur Rimbaud
location: Brussels, printed by the Alliance typographique (at Rimbaud's expense)
description: Une saison en enfer was written in 1873, partly at the family farm at Roche and partly in the aftermath of the shooting in Brussels that ended Rimbaud's relationship with Verlaine. It was printed in Brussels that October at his own expense, though he collected only a few copies and left the rest unpaid at the printer, where they were found in 1901. It is the only work Rimbaud himself published as a book. In a series of prose poems with interspersed verse, a speaker who calls himself damned recounts his revolt against Christianity, Western civilisation and his own bourgeois heritage, his imagined descent into savagery, and his visionary experiments with language in the section Alchemy of the Word. Delirium I, The Foolish Virgin and the Infernal Bridegroom, is often read as an account of his relationship with Verlaine. The work ends with a farewell and the declaration that one must be absolutely modern. Its fusion of confession, prophecy and fragmentary form had an immense influence on Symbolism and Surrealism.

title: Anna Karenina
creator: Leo Tolstoy
location: Moscow, serialised in The Russian Messenger (1875–77); book edition 1878
description: Anna Karenina opens with the famous sentence that all happy families are alike, but each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way. It was serialised from 1875 to 1877, though the editor refused to print the final part, which criticised Russian volunteers in the Serbian war, and Tolstoy published it separately. Anna, the beautiful wife of the senior official Alexei Karenin, meets the dashing officer Count Vronsky in Moscow, and they begin an affair that becomes the scandal of Saint Petersburg society. She leaves her husband and son to live with Vronsky, but excluded from society and consumed by jealousy, she throws herself under a train. Running parallel is the story of Konstantin Levin, an awkward landowner largely based on Tolstoy himself, who marries Kitty Shcherbatskaya, works alongside his peasants and struggles with questions of faith and death until he finds a kind of peace. Dostoevsky called it flawless as a work of art, and it is often named the greatest novel ever written.

title: A Doll's House
creator: Henrik Ibsen
location: Royal Danish Theatre, Copenhagen (21 December 1879)
description: A Doll's House was published in Copenhagen in December 1879 and premiered at the Royal Theatre there days later. Nora Helmer appears to be a happy, frivolous wife, indulged by her husband Torvald, a bank manager, who calls her his little lark and squirrel. But years earlier, to pay for a trip to Italy that saved Torvald's life, she secretly borrowed money by forging her dying father's signature. The lender, Krogstad, a disgraced employee at Torvald's bank, now threatens to expose her unless she saves his job. When Torvald reads Krogstad's letter, he furiously condemns her, then forgives her as soon as the danger passes. Nora realises that she has been a doll, first to her father and then to her husband, and that she must educate herself. In the famous final scene she leaves her husband and children, and the door slams behind her. The ending caused outrage, and for a German production Ibsen reluctantly wrote an alternative in which Nora stays. The play became a landmark of modern drama and of debates about women's rights.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
creator: Fyodor Dostoevsky
location: Moscow, serialised in The Russian Messenger
description: The Brothers Karamazov was serialised in 1879–80 and completed just months before Dostoevsky's death. In a provincial town, the buffoonish, lecherous landowner Fyodor Karamazov quarrels with his eldest son, the passionate army officer Dmitri, over money and the woman Grushenka. His second son Ivan is a brilliant sceptic, the youngest, Alyosha, a novice in the monastery of the holy elder Zosima, and the servant Smerdyakov is probably his illegitimate son. When Fyodor is murdered, Dmitri is arrested, tried and convicted, though the real killer was Smerdyakov, who claims he acted on Ivan's teaching that if there is no God everything is permitted. Ivan suffers a breakdown in which he converses with the devil. Within the novel, Ivan's prose poem The Grand Inquisitor, in which Christ returns to Seville during the Inquisition and is condemned by the church, is one of the most famous passages in literature. Freud called the novel the most magnificent ever written, and it is often regarded as Dostoevsky's masterpiece.

title: The Portrait of a Lady
creator: Henry James
location: Serialised in Macmillan's Magazine (London) and The Atlantic Monthly (Boston); book published by Macmillan, 1881
description: The Portrait of a Lady was serialised in 1880–81 and published as a book in 1881; James revised it extensively for the New York Edition of 1908. Isabel Archer, a spirited young American with little money, is brought to England by her aunt and refuses two proposals, from the English lord Warburton and the American businessman Caspar Goodwood, in order to keep her freedom. Her sickly cousin Ralph Touchett, who loves her, secretly persuades his dying father to leave her a large fortune so that she may live as she wishes. In Florence, Isabel is drawn by the worldly Madame Merle to Gilbert Osmond, a cultivated American expatriate, and marries him, only to find that he is cold and controlling and that he and Madame Merle were once lovers and are the parents of his daughter Pansy. Despite everything, Isabel returns to Rome and her marriage at the novel's end. The book's subtle tracing of consciousness, especially Isabel's long midnight meditation, made it one of James's masterpieces.

title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
creator: Mark Twain (Samuel Langhorne Clemens)
location: London (December 1884) and New York (February 1885), published by Chatto & Windus and Charles L. Webster
description: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn was published in Britain in December 1884 and in the United States in February 1885, with illustrations by E. W. Kemble. Told in Huck's own vernacular voice, it is set in the Mississippi valley before the Civil War. Huck, a boy who has been taken in by the Widow Douglas, is kidnapped by his drunken, violent father, fakes his own death and escapes to Jackson's Island, where he meets Jim, an enslaved man who has run away to avoid being sold. They travel down the river on a raft, encountering feuding families, a lynch mob and two con men who call themselves the King and the Duke and sell Jim. In a crisis of conscience, Huck decides that he will go to hell rather than betray Jim, and he tries to free him; Tom Sawyer reappears for a long, farcical rescue at the end. The novel's use of dialect and its satire of racism and hypocrisy made it a landmark of American literature, but its language and portrayal of Jim have made it one of the most frequently challenged books in American schools.

title: Germinal
creator: Émile Zola
location: Paris, serialised in Gil Blas (1884–85), then published by Charpentier
description: Germinal is the thirteenth novel of Zola's Rougon-Macquart cycle, serialised in 1884–85 and based on his visits to the coalfields of northern France, where he went down the pits and studied the strike at Anzin. Étienne Lantier, a young machinist who has been sacked for striking an employer, arrives at the mining village of Montsou and finds work at the Le Voreux pit, lodging with the Maheu family. He witnesses the hunger, exhaustion and danger of the miners' lives, falls in love with Catherine Maheu, and, inspired by socialist ideas, leads a strike when the company cuts wages. The strike leads to starvation, riot and the shooting of strikers by soldiers, and an anarchist sabotages the mine, which floods, trapping Étienne and Catherine underground. Étienne leaves at the end, sensing a new army germinating beneath the earth. The title refers to a month of the revolutionary calendar. The novel's power made it a classic of social fiction, and at Zola's funeral crowds of miners chanted its name.

title: The Death of Ivan Ilyich
creator: Leo Tolstoy
location: Moscow, in the twelfth volume of Tolstoy's collected works
description: The Death of Ivan Ilyich was published in 1886, the first major work of fiction Tolstoy wrote after the spiritual crisis described in his Confession. It begins with Ivan Ilyich's colleagues hearing of his death and thinking mainly of the promotions it will bring. Then it tells his life: a career as a magistrate pursued with propriety and ambition, a marriage that turns cold, and a comfortable home in Saint Petersburg. While hanging curtains he falls and injures his side, and an illness develops that no doctor can explain. As he suffers, he is tormented less by pain than by the lie that he is only ill, not dying, which his family and doctors maintain. Only his peasant servant Gerasim nurses him with simple honesty. In his last hours Ivan recognises that his life has not been what it should have been, feels pity for his family and dies in a moment of light. The novella is one of the most powerful meditations on death in literature.

title: Poems
creator: Emily Dickinson
location: Boston, published by Roberts Brothers (edited by Mabel Loomis Todd and T. W. Higginson)
description: Poems by Emily Dickinson was published in Boston in November 1890, four years after her death, and selected from the hundreds of manuscripts her sister Lavinia discovered. Its editors, Mabel Loomis Todd and Thomas Wentworth Higginson, arranged 115 poems under headings such as Life, Love, Nature and Time and Eternity, gave them titles and regularised much of her unconventional punctuation, rhyme and wording to suit contemporary taste. The book included poems now famous, such as Because I could not stop for Death, I never saw a moor and Success is counted sweetest. It sold well, going through eleven printings in two years, and was followed by second and third series in 1891 and 1896. Reviewers were divided, some praising her originality and others complaining of her roughness. Only with Thomas H. Johnson's complete edition of 1955 were the poems printed as she wrote them, with her characteristic dashes and capitals, revealing her as one of the most radical poets of the nineteenth century.

title: Hedda Gabler
creator: Henrik Ibsen
location: Residenztheater, Munich (31 January 1891); published Copenhagen, December 1890
description: Hedda Gabler was published in December 1890 and premiered in Munich in January 1891. Hedda, the proud daughter of the late General Gabler, has just returned from a long honeymoon with her husband Jørgen Tesman, an earnest, unremarkable academic hoping for a professorship, and she is already bored and trapped in their new house. Tesman's rival, Ejlert Løvborg, a brilliant former lover of Hedda's, has reformed with the help of the timid Thea Elvsted and written a visionary book. Out of jealousy and a desire to control another's fate, Hedda burns his only manuscript, after he loses it during a night of drinking, and gives him one of her father's pistols, urging him to die beautifully. Instead he is shot in a sordid accident, and Judge Brack, who knows the pistol was Hedda's, threatens to use the knowledge to dominate her. Rather than submit, Hedda shoots herself. The play's enigmatic heroine has become one of the great roles of the modern theatre.

title: Tess of the d'Urbervilles
creator: Thomas Hardy
location: London, serialised in The Graphic (with cuts) and published in three volumes by Osgood, McIlvaine
description: Tess of the d'Urbervilles: A Pure Woman Faithfully Presented was serialised in The Graphic in 1891 in a censored version and published in full later that year. Tess Durbeyfield, the daughter of a poor carter in rural Wessex, is sent to claim kinship with a wealthy family named d'Urberville after her father learns that they descend from an ancient Norman line. Alec d'Urberville, the family's son, seduces or rapes her, a matter the novel leaves deliberately ambiguous, and her baby dies. Working as a milkmaid at a dairy farm, she falls in love with Angel Clare, a clergyman's son, but on their wedding night, when she confesses her past, he abandons her. Reduced to hard labour and desperate to support her family, she returns to Alec. When Angel comes back repentant, she kills Alec and flees with Angel, but is captured at Stonehenge and hanged. Hardy's subtitle defied Victorian morality, and the novel's attack on sexual double standards caused a storm. It is now considered one of the great tragic novels.

title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
creator: Oscar Wilde
location: Lippincott's Monthly Magazine (July 1890); revised book edition, London, Ward, Lock & Co., 1891
description: The Picture of Dorian Gray was first published in the American Lippincott's Monthly Magazine in July 1890, where its editors cut passages they considered indecent. Reviewers attacked it as immoral, and Wilde expanded it to twenty chapters for the 1891 book edition, adding a preface of epigrams on art, including the claim that there is no such thing as a moral or an immoral book. The painter Basil Hallward completes a portrait of the beautiful young Dorian Gray, and the witty, cynical Lord Henry Wotton fills Dorian's head with a philosophy of pleasure and youth. Dorian wishes that the picture would age instead of him, and his wish is granted. He drives the actress Sibyl Vane to suicide, sinks into secret vice and murders Basil, while his face remains unspoiled and the hidden portrait grows hideous. Finally he stabs the picture and is found dead, withered and loathsome, beside the portrait restored to its original beauty. The novel was used against Wilde at his trials in 1895.

title: The Importance of Being Earnest
creator: Oscar Wilde
location: St James's Theatre, London (14 February 1895)
description: The Importance of Being Earnest: A Trivial Comedy for Serious People premiered at the St James's Theatre in London on 14 February 1895, just weeks before Wilde's arrest; the production was closed after his conviction. Jack Worthing, a respectable guardian in the country, has invented a dissolute younger brother, Ernest, whose name he uses in town. His friend Algernon Moncrieff has invented an invalid friend, Bunbury, whose illnesses let him escape dull engagements. Jack, as Ernest, proposes to Algernon's cousin Gwendolen, but her mother Lady Bracknell objects on learning that he was found as a baby in a handbag in the cloakroom at Victoria Station. Algernon, posing as Ernest, woos Jack's ward Cecily, and both young women have set their hearts on marrying a man called Ernest. The confusions are resolved when it is revealed that Jack is Algernon's elder brother and was in fact christened Ernest. With its perfect epigrams and absurd plot, the play is regarded as one of the greatest comedies in English.

title: The Seagull
creator: Anton Chekhov
location: Alexandrinsky Theatre, Saint Petersburg (17 October 1896); revived at the Moscow Art Theatre, 1898
description: The Seagull was first performed at the Alexandrinsky Theatre in Saint Petersburg in 1896, where the opening night was a disaster, the audience laughing in the wrong places, and Chekhov vowed never to write for the stage again. Two years later Konstantin Stanislavsky and Vladimir Nemirovich-Danchenko revived it at the newly founded Moscow Art Theatre, where its success established both the theatre and Chekhov's reputation; a seagull became the theatre's emblem. On the lakeside estate of Sorin, his nephew Konstantin Treplev stages an experimental play starring Nina, the girl he loves, which his mother, the famous actress Arkadina, mocks. Nina falls for Arkadina's lover, the successful writer Trigorin, who seduces and abandons her. Treplev shoots a seagull, which becomes a symbol of Nina's ruined life. Two years later she returns, a struggling actress, and after she leaves Treplev shoots himself offstage. Chekhov called it a comedy, and its mixture of the comic and the painful, and its subtext, changed modern drama.

title: The Turn of the Screw
creator: Henry James
location: Serialised in Collier's Weekly, New York; published in The Two Magics, 1898
description: The Turn of the Screw was serialised in Collier's Weekly in 1898 and published that year in The Two Magics. A frame narrator describes a gathering at which a man reads a manuscript left by his sister's former governess. The governess recounts how, as a young woman, she was hired by a man in London to take sole charge of his orphaned niece and nephew, Flora and Miles, at his country house of Bly, on condition that she never trouble him. She begins to see the figures of a man and a woman, whom the housekeeper identifies as the dead former valet Peter Quint and the previous governess Miss Jessel, and becomes convinced that their ghosts are corrupting the children. Her efforts to protect them lead to Flora's illness and, in the final scene, to Miles dying in her arms. Critics have debated for over a century whether the ghosts are real or the governess's delusions. The story inspired Britten's opera and many films.

title: Heart of Darkness
creator: Joseph Conrad
location: Blackwood's Magazine, Edinburgh (February–April 1899); book in Youth, 1902
description: Heart of Darkness was serialised in Blackwood's Magazine in 1899 and collected in Youth: A Narrative, and Two Other Stories in 1902. It draws on Conrad's own journey up the Congo River in 1890, in the Congo Free State controlled by King Leopold II of Belgium. On a yacht moored in the Thames at dusk, the sailor Marlow tells his companions of his experiences as a steamboat captain for a Belgian trading company. Travelling into Africa, he witnesses the brutality and absurdity of colonial exploitation and hears more and more about Kurtz, the company's most successful ivory agent, a man of great eloquence. When Marlow finally reaches the inner station, he finds Kurtz dying, surrounded by heads on stakes, having made himself a god to the local people. Kurtz's last words are The horror! The horror! Back in Europe, Marlow lies to Kurtz's fiancée about them. The novella is a central text of Modernism and of debates about colonialism, criticised by Chinua Achebe for its depiction of Africans, and it inspired the film Apocalypse Now.

title: Buddenbrooks
creator: Thomas Mann
location: Berlin, published by S. Fischer
description: Buddenbrooks: The Decline of a Family was published in two volumes in 1901, when Mann was twenty-six, and drew closely on the history of his own family of Lübeck grain merchants. The novel follows the Buddenbrooks from 1835, when they celebrate moving into a grand house, to 1877. The robust founder Johann is succeeded by his pious son Jean, then by the dutiful but increasingly exhausted Thomas, who becomes senator and keeps up appearances while his business falters, and finally by Thomas's son Hanno, a sickly, musically gifted boy who dies of typhoid as a teenager. Thomas's sister Tony, cheerful through two failed marriages, provides much of the comedy. Mann depicts the solid bourgeois world of a Hanseatic city in ironic, leisurely detail, while showing how its decline goes hand in hand with a growth of refinement, introspection and artistic feeling, influenced by Schopenhauer and Wagner. A cheap one-volume edition of 1903 became a bestseller, and the Nobel committee cited it specifically when awarding Mann the prize in 1929.

title: The Cherry Orchard
creator: Anton Chekhov
location: Moscow Art Theatre (17 January 1904)
description: The Cherry Orchard was Chekhov's last play, written while he was dying of tuberculosis and premiered by the Moscow Art Theatre on his name day in January 1904, months before his death. Lyubov Ranevskaya, a landowner who has squandered her fortune, returns from Paris to her family estate with her daughter Anya. The estate, with its famous cherry orchard, is to be auctioned to pay her debts. Lopakhin, a merchant whose father was a serf on the estate, urges her to cut down the orchard and lease the land for summer cottages, but she and her brother Gaev cannot bring themselves to act. At the auction Lopakhin buys the estate himself. The family departs, the ancient servant Firs is forgotten in the locked house, and the sound of axes is heard in the orchard. Chekhov insisted it was a comedy, and quarrelled with Stanislavsky over its tragic staging. It is often read as a portrait of the end of the Russian landed gentry and is one of the most performed plays of the modern repertory.

title: In Search of Lost Time
creator: Marcel Proust
location: Paris, Grasset (vol. 1, 1913) and Gallimard (vols 2–7, 1919–1927)
description: À la recherche du temps perdu, also translated as Remembrance of Things Past, was published in seven volumes: Swann's Way (1913), at Proust's own expense after rejections, including by André Gide at Gallimard; Within a Budding Grove (1919), which won the Prix Goncourt; The Guermantes Way; Sodom and Gomorrah; and, after Proust's death in 1922, The Captive, The Fugitive and Time Regained, edited from his manuscripts. Its narrator, Marcel, recalls his childhood in the village of Combray, brought back whole by the taste of a madeleine dipped in lime-blossom tea; the earlier love affair of the elegant Charles Swann with the courtesan Odette; his own adolescent love for Gilberte and later for the elusive Albertine; his entry into the aristocratic world of the Guermantes; and the figures of the Baron de Charlus and the painter Elstir. At a final reception after the First World War, he realises through involuntary memory that his vocation is to write the book we have just read. Its long sentences and its analysis of time and consciousness made it one of the defining works of Modernism.

title: Dubliners
creator: James Joyce
location: London, published by Grant Richards
description: Dubliners was written mainly in 1904–07, but its publication was delayed for nearly a decade as publishers and printers objected to its frankness, its use of real names and places and its references to Edward VII; one printer destroyed the sheets. It finally appeared in London in 1914. Joyce described its plan as a chapter of the moral history of his country and said he wanted to present Dublin as the centre of paralysis. The fifteen stories are arranged to move from childhood, as in The Sisters and Araby, through adolescence and maturity to public life, and are written in what he called a style of scrupulous meanness. Many end in a moment of sudden revelation, which Joyce called an epiphany. The final story, The Dead, set at a Christmas party, ends with Gabriel Conroy learning of his wife's long-dead young lover and contemplating the snow falling all over Ireland. The collection is one of the most influential in the history of the short story.

title: The Metamorphosis
creator: Franz Kafka
location: Die weißen Blätter (October 1915); book published by Kurt Wolff, Leipzig, 1915
description: The Metamorphosis (Die Verwandlung) was written in late 1912 and published in 1915. Its first sentence, in which Gregor Samsa wakes from uneasy dreams to find himself transformed into an enormous vermin, is among the most famous in literature. Gregor, a travelling salesman who supports his parents and sister by a job he hates, worries at first mainly about being late for work. His family are horrified; his father drives him back into his room and later wounds him with an apple that lodges in his back. His sister Grete feeds him, but over time the family grows resentful as they are forced to take jobs and take in lodgers. When Grete declares that the creature must go, Gregor, weakened, dies alone, and the relieved family take a trip to the country, noticing that Grete has become a young woman. Kafka insisted that the insect should never be drawn on the cover. The story has been read as a parable of alienation, family, illness and capitalism, and is one of the most widely read works of the century.

title: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock
creator: T. S. Eliot
location: Poetry magazine, Chicago (June 1915); collected in Prufrock and Other Observations, London, 1917
description: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock was written mostly in 1910–11, while Eliot was a student, and published in Chicago's Poetry magazine in 1915 after Ezra Pound pressed its editor, Harriet Monroe, to accept it. It became the title poem of Eliot's first collection in 1917. Prufrock, a self-conscious, middle-aged man, invites an unnamed companion to go with him through half-deserted streets to a drawing-room where the women come and go talking of Michelangelo. He circles around an overwhelming question, probably a declaration of love, but is paralysed by self-doubt, measuring out his life with coffee spoons, imagining the mockery of others, and ending with a vision of mermaids who will not sing to him. Its epigraph from Dante, ironic juxtapositions, abrupt shifts and urban imagery, influenced by the French Symbolist Jules Laforgue, marked a radical break with Victorian and Georgian poetry. It is often regarded as the beginning of Modernist poetry in English.

title: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
creator: James Joyce
location: Serialised in The Egoist, London (1914–15); book published by B. W. Huebsch, New York, 1916
description: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man grew out of an earlier, abandoned novel, Stephen Hero, and was serialised in the London magazine The Egoist in 1914–15 with the help of Ezra Pound, then published as a book in New York in 1916. It follows Stephen Dedalus, Joyce's fictional double, from his earliest memories, rendered in the language of a small child, through his Jesuit schooling at Clongowes and Belvedere, a famous Christmas dinner argument over the fall of the nationalist leader Parnell, his adolescent sexual awakening, terror at a sermon on hell and a period of intense piety. A vision of a girl wading on a beach confirms his vocation as an artist, and at University College he develops a theory of aesthetics and resolves to leave Ireland, using silence, exile and cunning as his weapons. The prose style develops with Stephen's mind, an early form of stream of consciousness. The novel is a founding Modernist Künstlerroman, and Stephen reappears in Ulysses.

title: The Second Coming
creator: W. B. Yeats
location: The Dial (November 1920); collected in Michael Robartes and the Dancer, 1921
description: The Second Coming was written in January 1919, in the aftermath of the First World War, the Russian Revolution and the Easter Rising, and first published in The Dial in 1920. In twenty-two lines of loose blank verse, Yeats describes a world in which things fall apart and the centre cannot hold, the falcon cannot hear the falconer, and anarchy is loosed upon the world. The speaker then has a vision of a figure with a lion's body and the head of a man rising from the desert, and asks what rough beast, its hour come round at last, slouches towards Bethlehem to be born. The poem draws on Yeats's cyclical theory of history, later set out in A Vision, in which the two-thousand-year Christian era is ending and giving way to its opposite, symbolised by interlocking gyres. It is one of the most quoted poems of the twentieth century, its phrases borrowed for many book titles, among them Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart.

title: Ulysses
creator: James Joyce
location: Paris, published by Shakespeare and Company (Sylvia Beach), 2 February 1922
description: Ulysses was written between 1914 and 1921 in Trieste, Zurich and Paris. Parts were serialised in the American Little Review, whose editors were convicted of obscenity in 1921, and the book was published in Paris by Sylvia Beach on Joyce's fortieth birthday. It was banned in the United States until a court ruled in 1933 that it was not obscene. Its eighteen episodes, each loosely corresponding to an episode of the Odyssey, follow a single day, 16 June 1904. Leopold Bloom, a Jewish advertising canvasser, goes about his business, attends a funeral, visits a newspaper office, a pub, a maternity hospital and the brothel district, aware that his wife Molly is about to begin an affair. His wanderings cross those of the young Stephen Dedalus, and late at night Bloom takes Stephen home. The book ends with Molly's unpunctuated monologue, which closes on her word yes. Each episode uses a different style, from stream of consciousness to parody and a play script. Ulysses is widely regarded as the most important novel of the twentieth century.

title: The Waste Land
creator: T. S. Eliot
location: The Criterion, London (October 1922) and The Dial, New York (November 1922); book by Boni & Liveright, December 1922
description: The Waste Land was published in 1922, the same year as Ulysses, first in Eliot's own magazine The Criterion and in the American Dial, and then as a book with Eliot's notes. Much of it was written in 1921 while Eliot was recovering from a breakdown in Margate and Lausanne, and Ezra Pound's drastic editing of the manuscript, which survived and was published in 1971, cut it nearly in half; Eliot dedicated it to Pound as the better craftsman. In five sections, The Burial of the Dead, A Game of Chess, The Fire Sermon, Death by Water and What the Thunder Said, its 434 lines move abruptly between voices, languages and scenes: a crowd flowing over London Bridge, a neurotic couple, a pub conversation, a typist's loveless encounter, and a journey through a dry landscape. It draws on the Grail legend, fertility myth, Dante, Shakespeare, the Upanishads and dozens of other sources. Its fragmentation and allusiveness defined Modernist poetry and influenced generations of writers.

title: Duino Elegies
creator: Rainer Maria Rilke
location: Leipzig, published by Insel Verlag
description: The Duino Elegies take their name from Duino Castle on the Adriatic near Trieste, where Rilke was a guest of Princess Marie von Thurn und Taxis in early 1912. According to the princess's account, he was walking on the cliffs in a strong wind when he heard the line that opens the first elegy, asking who, if he cried out, would hear him among the angelic orders. He wrote two elegies there, but the sequence stalled for ten years through the war and personal crisis, until, at the Château de Muzot in Switzerland in February 1922, he completed the remaining elegies in a few weeks, along with the Sonnets to Orpheus. Published in 1923, the ten elegies confront the gulf between human beings and the terrifying angels, the transience of love, the figures of lovers, heroes, children and acrobats, and death; they move from lament towards praise, suggesting that our task is to say things, house, bridge, fountain, and so transform the visible into the invisible within us. They are among the most admired poems of the twentieth century.

title: The Magic Mountain
creator: Thomas Mann
location: Berlin, published by S. Fischer
description: The Magic Mountain was begun in 1912, after Mann visited his wife at a sanatorium in Davos, interrupted by the First World War and published in two volumes in 1924. Hans Castorp, an ordinary young engineer from Hamburg, travels to the International Sanatorium Berghof in the Swiss Alps to visit his cousin Joachim, a patient. Found to have a spot on his lung himself, he remains for seven years, in a world where time loses its meaning. He falls in love with the Russian Clavdia Chauchat and is educated by two rival mentors, the Italian humanist Settembrini, who champions reason and progress, and the Jesuit-trained Naphta, who argues for terror and absolutism; later he meets the overwhelming Dutch planter Peeperkorn. In a snowstorm, Hans has a visionary dream about love and death. The outbreak of war in 1914 finally ends his stay, and the novel leaves him on a battlefield. It is a great novel of ideas and a portrait of pre-war European culture, and an ironic version of the Bildungsroman.

title: Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair
creator: Pablo Neruda
location: Santiago, published by Nascimento
description: Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair was published in Santiago in 1924, when Neruda was nineteen, and caused a scandal for its eroticism before becoming one of the most widely read books of poetry ever written in Spanish, with millions of copies sold. The poems are addressed to women Neruda loved as a student in Temuco and Santiago, merged into a single beloved whose body is compared to the earth, the sea, the night and the landscapes of southern Chile. They move between desire, possession, absence and loss, and include the famous Poem 20, which begins by saying the poet can write the saddest lines tonight. The final Song of Despair laments abandonment against the image of a harbour at dawn. Written in long, rhythmic free and loosely metrical lines, the poems combine late Romantic and Modernist influences with a fresh, direct sensuality. They made Neruda a celebrated poet across Latin America at the start of his career.

title: The Trial
creator: Franz Kafka
location: Berlin, published by Die Schmiede (edited by Max Brod)
description: The Trial (Der Process) was written in 1914–15 and left unfinished, its chapters in a loose order, and was published by Kafka's friend Max Brod in 1925, against Kafka's instruction to burn his manuscripts. On the morning of his thirtieth birthday, Josef K., a bank official, is arrested in his lodgings by two warders, though he is allowed to continue working. The charge is never revealed. He attends a hearing in a tenement attic and discovers that the court has offices in attics throughout the city, staffed by corrupt and lecherous officials. A sickly lawyer, a painter who paints the judges and various women offer help that leads nowhere. In the cathedral a priest tells him the parable Before the Law, in which a man waits all his life at a door meant only for him. On the eve of his thirty-first birthday, two men take K. to a quarry and kill him like a dog, as he says. The novel's vision of opaque, inescapable authority gave the word Kafkaesque its meaning.

title: Mrs Dalloway
creator: Virginia Woolf
location: London, published by the Hogarth Press
description: Mrs Dalloway was published by the Hogarth Press, which Woolf and her husband ran, in May 1925. Its working title was The Hours. The novel follows a single day in London in June 1923. Clarissa Dalloway, the wife of a Conservative MP, walks through Westminster to buy flowers for her party that evening, and her thoughts move back to her youth at Bourton and her love for Peter Walsh, who unexpectedly visits, and for Sally Seton. Interwoven with her day is that of Septimus Warren Smith, a veteran suffering from shell shock, who hears birds singing in Greek and whose doctors fail him; to avoid being committed, he throws himself from a window. At the party Clarissa hears of his death and feels a strange kinship with him. Woolf moves fluidly between characters' minds, using Big Ben's chimes to mark time. The novel is a landmark of Modernism, and Michael Cunningham's novel The Hours retold it.

title: The Great Gatsby
creator: F. Scott Fitzgerald
location: New York, published by Charles Scribner's Sons
description: The Great Gatsby was published in April 1925, with a famous cover by Francis Cugat showing a woman's face above the lights of an amusement park. It is narrated by Nick Carraway, a young Midwesterner who moves to West Egg on Long Island in the summer of 1922 to work in bonds. His neighbour is Jay Gatsby, a fabulously wealthy and mysterious man who throws enormous parties. Gatsby, it emerges, was born James Gatz to poor farmers and made his fortune in bootlegging, all to win back Daisy, Nick's cousin, whom he loved as a young officer and who is now married to the brutal, rich Tom Buchanan. Gatsby and Daisy resume their affair, but in a confrontation at the Plaza Hotel she chooses Tom. Driving Gatsby's car, Daisy kills Tom's mistress Myrtle, and Myrtle's husband shoots Gatsby, who dies alone. Fitzgerald's lyrical prose and his portrait of the Jazz Age and the corruption of the American Dream made the novel, which sold poorly at first, one of the most celebrated works of American literature.

title: The Sun Also Rises
creator: Ernest Hemingway
location: New York, published by Charles Scribner's Sons
description: The Sun Also Rises was published in October 1926 and based closely on a trip Hemingway and friends made to the fiesta of San Fermín in Pamplona in 1925. Its epigraphs set Gertrude Stein's remark, you are all a lost generation, against a passage from Ecclesiastes. The narrator, Jake Barnes, an American journalist in Paris, has been left impotent by a war wound and is in love with Lady Brett Ashley, a charming, promiscuous Englishwoman who loves him but will not live without sex. With Brett's fiancé Mike, the insecure Jewish writer Robert Cohn, who has had an affair with Brett, and Jake's friend Bill, they travel to Spain, fish in the Pyrenees and attend the bullfights in Pamplona, where Brett runs off with the young bullfighter Pedro Romero. The novel's stripped-down prose and understated dialogue made Hemingway's reputation and defined the disillusioned expatriate generation, though its portrayal of Cohn has been criticised as antisemitic.

title: To the Lighthouse
creator: Virginia Woolf
location: London, published by the Hogarth Press
description: To the Lighthouse was published in May 1927 and draws on Woolf's childhood summers at Talland House in Cornwall and on her parents, Leslie and Julia Stephen. The novel is in three parts. The Window takes place on a single day before the First World War at the Ramsays' holiday house on the Isle of Skye: young James longs to visit the lighthouse, his philosopher father insists the weather will be bad, and Mrs Ramsay, the warm centre of the household, presides over a dinner party, while the painter Lily Briscoe struggles with her picture. The short middle section, Time Passes, describes the empty house over ten years, during which Mrs Ramsay, her daughter Prue and her son Andrew die, the last in the war, events reported in brackets. In The Lighthouse, Mr Ramsay finally sails there with his now adolescent children, while Lily, on the lawn, completes her painting in a moment of vision. The novel's lyrical treatment of time, memory and art makes it Woolf's masterpiece for many readers.

title: The Sound and the Fury
creator: William Faulkner
location: New York, published by Jonathan Cape and Harrison Smith
description: The Sound and the Fury was published in October 1929; its title comes from Macbeth's speech about life as a tale told by an idiot. It tells the story of the Compsons, an old Southern family in decay in Jefferson, Mississippi, in four sections. The first is narrated by Benjy, a thirty-three-year-old man with a severe cognitive disability, whose mind moves without distinction between past and present, on 7 April 1928. The second follows his brother Quentin, a Harvard student, on 2 June 1910, the day of his suicide, obsessed with their sister Caddy's lost virginity. The third is told by the bitter, scheming brother Jason in 1928, and the fourth, in the third person, centres on Dilsey, the family's Black servant, on Easter Sunday 1928, as Caddy's daughter Quentin runs away with Jason's money. The novel's stream of consciousness, fractured chronology and density made it difficult for its first readers, but it is now considered one of the greatest American novels.

title: The Stranger
creator: Albert Camus
location: Paris, published by Gallimard
description: The Stranger (L'Étranger, also translated as The Outsider) was published by Gallimard in occupied Paris in 1942, the same year as Camus's essay The Myth of Sisyphus. It opens with the flat statement that Mother died today, or maybe yesterday. Meursault, a shipping clerk in Algiers, attends his mother's funeral without showing emotion, begins an affair the next day, and becomes involved in the quarrels of his neighbour Raymond. On a blindingly hot beach, he shoots an Arab man who had fought with Raymond, firing four more shots into the body for no reason he can explain. At his trial the prosecution concentrates on his indifference at the funeral, and he is sentenced to death. In his cell, after angrily rejecting a chaplain's offer of faith, he opens himself to the benign indifference of the universe. Written in short, plain sentences, the novel became a classic of absurdist literature. Kamel Daoud's novel The Meursault Investigation (2013) retold it from the perspective of the victim's brother.

title: Ficciones
creator: Jorge Luis Borges
location: Buenos Aires, published by Sur
description: Ficciones brings together two earlier collections, The Garden of Forking Paths (1941) and Artifices (1944), and was expanded in 1956. Its stories include Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius, in which an imaginary world described in a pirated encyclopaedia gradually takes over the real one; Pierre Menard, Author of the Quixote, a mock review of a writer who rewrites Cervantes word for word; The Library of Babel, an infinite library containing every possible book; The Garden of Forking Paths, a spy story built around a novel in which all possible outcomes occur; Funes the Memorious, about a man who forgets nothing; and The Lottery in Babylon and Death and the Compass. Combining the forms of the essay, the detective story and the philosophical puzzle, the stories explore infinity, time, identity and the nature of fiction itself. The collection made Borges internationally famous, especially after its translation in the 1960s, and was a key influence on postmodern literature and the Latin American Boom.

title: Animal Farm
creator: George Orwell (Eric Arthur Blair)
location: London, published by Secker & Warburg
description: Animal Farm: A Fairy Story was written in 1943–44 and rejected by several publishers, including T. S. Eliot at Faber, because Britain was then allied with the Soviet Union; it was published in August 1945. Inspired by the old boar Old Major's dream of a world without humans, the animals of Manor Farm rebel and drive out the drunken farmer Jones, renaming it Animal Farm and adopting Seven Commandments, including that all animals are equal. The pigs take charge, and the idealistic Snowball is driven out by the ruthless Napoleon, who uses dogs as secret police, rewrites history through his propagandist Squealer and exploits the loyal carthorse Boxer until he is sold to the knacker. The commandments are gradually altered until only one remains: all animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others. At the end the pigs walk on two legs and dine with the farmers, indistinguishable from them. The fable is a satire on Stalinism and on the betrayal of revolutionary ideals, and it was Orwell's first great success.

title: The Plague
creator: Albert Camus
location: Paris, published by Gallimard
description: The Plague (La Peste) was published in 1947 and was an immediate success. It is presented as a chronicle of an epidemic of bubonic plague in the Algerian coastal city of Oran in the 1940s, narrated by someone who turns out to be Dr Bernard Rieux. Rats die in the streets, then people, and the authorities reluctantly close the city. Cut off from the world, the inhabitants respond in different ways: Rieux simply does his job of treating the sick; the visitor Tarrou organises volunteer sanitary teams; the journalist Rambert tries to escape to his lover in Paris but stays to help; the priest Paneloux preaches that the plague is God's punishment, until the agonising death of a child shakes him; and the petty criminal Cottard thrives on the crisis. After almost a year the plague recedes, but Rieux warns that the bacillus never dies. The novel is widely read as an allegory of the German occupation of France and of the human response to evil and suffering, and it found new readers during the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Nineteen Eighty-Four
creator: George Orwell (Eric Arthur Blair)
location: London, published by Secker & Warburg
description: Nineteen Eighty-Four was written on the Scottish island of Jura while Orwell was gravely ill with tuberculosis and published in June 1949, seven months before his death. Britain, now Airstrip One, is a province of Oceania, a super-state perpetually at war and ruled by the Party under the image of Big Brother, whose face is everywhere above the slogan that Big Brother is watching you. Winston Smith works at the Ministry of Truth rewriting old newspapers to match the Party's changing version of history. He begins a secret diary and a forbidden love affair with Julia, and believes that O'Brien, an Inner Party member, belongs to a resistance movement. But O'Brien is a loyal agent; Winston and Julia are arrested, and in the Ministry of Love Winston is tortured until, in Room 101, he betrays Julia and comes to love Big Brother. The novel's vision of surveillance, propaganda and the destruction of truth, and its invented language Newspeak, made it one of the most influential novels of the twentieth century.

title: Waiting for Godot
creator: Samuel Beckett
location: Théâtre de Babylone, Paris (5 January 1953)
description: Waiting for Godot was written in French as En attendant Godot in 1948–49, published in 1952 and premiered at the small Théâtre de Babylone in Paris in January 1953; Beckett's own English translation was first staged in London in 1955. On a country road by a single tree, two tramps, Vladimir and Estragon, wait for a man called Godot, whom they have apparently arranged to meet. To pass the time they talk, quarrel, eat a carrot, consider hanging themselves and play verbal games. They are visited by the tyrannical Pozzo and his slave Lucky, whom he drives on a rope, and who delivers a torrent of garbled philosophy when ordered to think. At the end of each act a boy arrives to say that Godot will not come today but surely tomorrow. The second act repeats the first with variations, and the play ends with the two agreeing to go, and not moving. One critic famously described it as a play in which nothing happens, twice. Its mixture of vaudeville, bleak humour and metaphysical anguish made it the defining work of the Theatre of the Absurd.

title: Lolita
creator: Vladimir Nabokov
location: Paris, published by Olympia Press; first US edition, G. P. Putnam's Sons, 1958
description: Lolita was rejected by several American publishers and first published in Paris in 1955 by Olympia Press, which specialised in erotic and avant-garde books. Graham Greene's praise and the ensuing controversy made it notorious, and its American publication in 1958 made it a bestseller. Framed as the prison memoir of Humbert Humbert, a European émigré scholar, it tells how he marries Charlotte Haze to be near her twelve-year-old daughter Dolores, whom he calls Lolita. After Charlotte's accidental death he takes the girl on a long road trip across America, abusing her in motel after motel, until she escapes with the playwright Clare Quilty, whom Humbert eventually tracks down and murders. Nabokov's virtuoso, playful prose and Humbert's seductive, self-justifying voice force readers to see through his rhetoric to the suffering of the child he has destroyed. The novel remains controversial, but it is widely regarded as one of the masterpieces of twentieth-century fiction.

title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
creator: Gabriel García Márquez
location: Buenos Aires, published by Editorial Sudamericana
description: One Hundred Years of Solitude (Cien años de soledad) was written in Mexico City and published in Buenos Aires in May 1967, where its first printing sold out within weeks; it went on to sell tens of millions of copies in many languages. It tells the history of the town of Macondo, founded in a swamp by José Arcadio Buendía and his wife Úrsula Iguarán, and of seven generations of their descendants, whose names, José Arcadio and Aureliano, repeat as their characters and fates do. Colonel Aureliano Buendía fights thirty-two civil wars and loses them all; a plague of insomnia causes the town to forget the names of things; a beautiful girl ascends to heaven while hanging out the laundry; and a banana company brings foreign exploitation and a massacre of striking workers that the authorities deny ever happened. In the end the last Buendía deciphers the manuscripts of the gypsy Melquíades, which foretold the family's whole history, as a wind wipes Macondo away. The novel's magical realism made it the emblem of the Latin American Boom.

title: Invisible Cities
creator: Italo Calvino
location: Turin, published by Einaudi
description: Invisible Cities (Le città invisibili) was published in 1972. Its frame is a series of conversations between the Venetian traveller Marco Polo and the aged Tartar emperor Kublai Khan, who is trying to understand the vast empire he can never see for himself. Between these dialogues, Polo describes fifty-five cities, each with a woman's name, grouped under headings such as Cities and Memory, Cities and Desire, Cities and Signs, Thin Cities, Trading Cities, Cities and the Dead and Hidden Cities. There is a city suspended over an abyss on a net, a city whose inhabitants rebuild it continually, a city that exists only as a reflection, and a city made of nothing but water pipes. The book's mathematical structure reflects Calvino's links with the Oulipo, and as the dialogues proceed it emerges that every city Polo describes may be Venice. Short prose poems rather than a conventional narrative, the cities have inspired architects, urbanists and artists as well as readers of fiction.

title: Beloved
creator: Toni Morrison
location: New York, published by Alfred A. Knopf
description: Beloved was published in 1987 and won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1988. It was inspired by the story of Margaret Garner, an enslaved woman who escaped from Kentucky to Ohio in 1856 and killed her daughter rather than let her be recaptured. In 1873, near Cincinnati, Sethe lives with her daughter Denver at 124 Bluestone Road, a house haunted by the angry spirit of a baby. When Paul D, a man from the Kentucky plantation called Sweet Home where they were both enslaved, arrives, he drives the ghost out. Soon afterwards, a mysterious young woman who calls herself Beloved appears, and Sethe comes to believe that she is the daughter she killed eighteen years earlier. Through fragmented memories, the novel gradually reveals the horrors of slavery and what Sethe did, as Beloved's presence consumes her mother, until the community of women gathers to drive her away. Its lyrical, many-voiced prose and its confrontation with the legacy of slavery made it one of the most acclaimed American novels of its time.
